blogs/hackathon/my-first-hackathon.html:
Yesterday at the CSHub Local Hack Day, my first hackathon ever, my teammate Soroush Baraouf and I challenged ourselves to build a fully functional product in just one day.

The Result: Meet "HawkEye" 🚀

Resellers spend hours manually logging inventory. HawkEye changes that. You simply record a video pan of a clothing rack, and our AI analyzes the footage. It identifies items (e.g., "Vintage Levi's 501"), detects specific damage like a missing button, and instantly estimates market value.

My project role:

  • Frontend & UX: Designed the user interface and overall experience.

The Challenge: Raw Video Processing

The main technical hurdle was processing raw video for the #GoogleGemini 2.5 Flash API.

The Fix: I built an #FFmpeg pipeline to extract frames and timestamps, enabling Gemini to process video at a granular level for deeper analysis. This unlocked a full spectrum of Gemini’s multimodal capabilities: video understanding, image interpretation, voice detection, text generation, reasoning, and real-time data retrieval.

How Gemini Powers the Backend

  • Analyze video frames and identify items with high accuracy
  • Detect condition details like missing buttons or wear
  • Interpret audio cues (if present)
  • Search the web for live market prices
  • Reason about value ranges and suggest a lower and higher price based on condition
  • Generate optimized listing descriptions for online marketplaces

We designed the pipeline so Gemini acts as the backbone of our product and an end-to-end assistant, from visual understanding to pricing intelligence to marketplace-ready text.

Deployment & The "Meta" Twist

The application was containerized with Docker and deployed on Render.

But here is the "Meta" twist: We didn't just use AI; we built with it. We utilized the #GeminiCLI (my favorite new AI toy) as an agentic assistant to handle boilerplate code and rapid debugging, allowing us to hit the strict 12-hour deadline.

A huge thanks to my teammate Soroush Baraouf for the incredible collaboration. Going from zero code to execution in 12 hours was an intense but rewarding experience.

blogs/hackathon/my-second-hackathon.title: Undercut: Building a Production-Grade AI Car Platform
blogs/hackathon/my-second-hackathon.html:
For my second hackathon, my teammates Soroush Baraouf, Parisa Taherizadeh, Ariyan Azami, and Mahan Ghaffarianmayouni and I took on an ambitious challenge: building a full-stack, production-ready platform that uses AI and quantitative analysis to help people find underpriced used cars in the Toronto market.

The Result: Meet "Undercut" 🚗

The used car market is notoriously opaque. Buyers lack tools to determine if a listing is fairly priced or a potential scam. Undercut levels the playing field by combining high-frequency web scraping, quantitative pricing algorithms, and Google Gemini AI analysis to give buyers "unfair" market intelligence.

My project role:

  • Scraper Developer: Engineered high-performance scrapers in Go with Playwright to extract real-time data for thousands of GTA car listings.
  • Backend Architecture: Designed and built the FastAPI backend with SQLAlchemy ORM.
  • AI Integration: Implemented Google Gemini 1.5 Flash for listing analysis and negotiation scripts.
  • Quantitative Engine: Developed Fair Market Value (FMV) calculation and deal grading algorithms.

The Challenge: Building a Complete Ecosystem

Unlike a typical hackathon project, Undercut required building three interconnected systems:

1. The Scraper ("The Hunter") - Go

Built with Playwright for Go, I developed the scraper that navigates AutoTrader.ca to extract car listings. The main challenge was bypassing anti-bot protections on a JavaScript-heavy site. I implemented stealth techniques and headless browser automation to scrape thousands of listings within a 100km radius of Toronto (GTA).

2. The Backend ("The Controller") - Python FastAPI

The backend is the brain of Undercut. I architected a FastAPI application with:

  • SQLAlchemy ORM for database interactions with PostgreSQL
  • Pydantic schemas for type-safe request/response validation
  • Rate limiting using SlowAPI to prevent abuse
  • Comprehensive REST API with 15+ endpoints for cars, users, and alerts
  • Quantitative services for FMV calculation and deal grading (S/A/B/C/F tiers)

3. The Frontend - Next.js 14

My teammate built a modern React interface using Next.js 14 with the App Router, featuring:

  • Server-side rendering for optimal performance
  • Radix UI components for accessibility
  • Framer Motion animations for smooth interactions
  • TanStack Query for efficient data fetching

The AI Integration: Gemini as "The Mechanic"

I integrated Google Gemini 1.5 Flash to power two critical features:

Red Flag Detection

The AI scans seller descriptions for concerning keywords like "rebuilt title," "needs work," or "running rough." It acts as a virtual expert mechanic, providing instant verdicts on whether a deal is worth pursuing.

Negotiation Script Generator

Once a user finds a car, Gemini generates a personalized negotiation script. It includes:

  • Specific data points from our FMV analysis
  • A suggested opening offer price
  • Key leverage points based on market data
  • A walk-away threshold

The prompt engineering was critical. I designed the system prompt to make Gemini act as a "ruthless expert car flipper," ensuring unbiased, profit-focused analysis.

The Quantitative Engine

I built a custom pricing algorithm that calculates Fair Market Value (FMV) for each listing. The system then assigns a deal grade:

  • S-Tier: 10%+ below FMV (exceptional opportunity)
  • A-Tier: 5-10% below FMV (great deal)
  • B-Tier: Within 5% of FMV (fair price)
  • C-Tier: 5-10% above FMV (overpriced)
  • F-Tier: 10%+ above FMV (avoid)

Additionally, I implemented a Total Cost of Ownership (TCO) calculator that factors in fuel costs, depreciation, insurance, and maintenance to show users the real monthly cost of ownership.

Database Design & Architecture

The application uses PostgreSQL hosted on Supabase. I designed a normalized schema with four main tables:

  • cars: Stores all scraped listings with VIN indexing
  • users: User profiles with onboarding completion tracking
  • alerts: "Sniper alerts" for instant notifications on new deals
  • saved_cars: Junction table for user watchlists

Testing & Quality Assurance

I wrote a comprehensive test suite using pytest, covering:

  • Unit tests for all CRUD endpoints
  • Service layer tests for FMV, TCO, and deal grading
  • Integration tests for search and trending features
  • Mock AI responses to avoid API costs during testing

Deployment & DevOps

The entire stack is containerized with Docker and orchestrated using Docker Compose. The frontend is deployed on Vercel, while the backend and scraper run on managed cloud infrastructure.

This hackathon taught me the importance of system design, API architecture, and building production-grade features under pressure. A huge thanks to my teammates Soroush Baraouf, Parisa Taherizadeh, Ariyan Azami, and Mahan Ghaffarianmayouni for the incredible collaboration. Building a full-stack AI platform from scratch was the most challenging and rewarding coding experience I've had.

learning/deep-learning/blocks/block01.title: Foundations of Neural Networks
learning/deep-learning/blocks/block01.description: If this foundation is strong, deep learning becomes logical. If it is weak, everything later will feel like magic.
learning/deep-learning/blocks/block01.html:
Biological vs. Artificial

The artificial neuron is inspired by the biological version. It receives signals, processes them, and fires if the total signal strength exceeds a threshold.

Biological

Signals enter through Dendrites, are summed in the Cell Body, and travel down the Axon if threshold is met.

Artificial

Inputs are multiplied by Weights, added to a Bias, and passed through an Activation Function.

The Core Equation

Everything in Deep Learning stems from this single formula:

y = f(w · x + b)

x

Inputs (Features)

Raw data points, like pixel values or student GPA.

w

Weights (Importance)

The learned parameters that determine how much each input matters.

b

Bias (Shift)

Allows the model to shift the activation function for better flexibility.

Activation: Why Linearity Fails

Real-world data is rarely a straight line. Activation functions add Non-linearity, allowing the network to solve complex problems like image recognition.

// Python implementation (The Pure Way) def neuron(x, w, b): # Weighted Sum (Dot Product) z = sum(xi * wi for xi, wi in zip(x, w)) + b # Simple threshold activation return 1 if z > 0 else 0 # Example inputs = [2, 3] weights = [0.5, 1.0] bias = 1 print(neuron(inputs, weights, bias)) # Result: 1

learning/deep-learning/blocks/block02.title: Activation Functions
learning/deep-learning/blocks/block02.description: The "Soul" of Deep Learning. Without these tiny nonlinear functions, neural networks would be nothing more than basic linear regression.
learning/deep-learning/blocks/block02.html:
The Problem of Linearity

Recall the neuron output: $z = w \cdot x + b$. This is a linear equation. If we stack layers without activation, the entire network collapses into a single linear transformation, making it impossible to learn complex patterns.

"Think of activations as gates: Closed (ignore signal), Half-open (weak signal), or Fully open (strong signal). Without gates, every neuron talks at once—creating noise, not learning."

Key Activation Functions

Sigmoid

$\sigma(z) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-z}}$

Outputs (0, 1). Great for probabilities in the final layer, but suffers from Vanishing Gradients in hidden layers.

ReLU

Game Changer

$f(z) = \max(0, z)$

Simple and fast. Reduces vanishing gradients. The standard default for hidden layers since 2012.

Tanh

$f(z) = \tanh(z)$

Outputs (-1, 1). Zero-centered, which helps the model learn faster than sigmoid, but still saturates at extremes.

Leaky ReLU

$f(z) = z \text{ if } z > 0, \text{ else } 0.01z$

Fixes the "Dying ReLU" problem by allowing a small, non-zero gradient when input is negative.

Selection Strategy

Layer Type Recommended Activation
Hidden Layers ReLU or Leaky ReLU
Binary Classification Output Sigmoid
Multi-class Output Softmax
Regression Output Linear (None)

Softmax Intuition

Used in the Output Layer ONLY for multi-class classification. It converts raw scores (logits) into a probability distribution that sums to 1.

// Activation Logic in Python import math def relu(z): return max(0, z) def sigmoid(z): return 1 / (1 + math.exp(-z)) # Softmax highlights the strongest class scores = [2.1, 1.2, 0.3] # Result: [0.65, 0.24, 0.11] (probabilities sum to 1)

Block 2 Review

Explain the Vanishing Gradient problem
Why ReLU is more computationally efficient
Differentiate Sigmoid vs Softmax use cases
The concept of "Dying ReLU" neurons

learning/deep-learning/blocks/block03.title: Artificial Neural Networks
learning/deep-learning/blocks/block03.description: This is where single neurons become intelligence. We move from individual units to a stacked architecture capable of modeling the world.
learning/deep-learning/blocks/block03.html:
ANN Anatomy

An ANN is a hierarchical stack of layers. Each layer extracts progressively more complex features from the data.

Input Layer

Holds raw data (pixels, features). No computation happens here; it's simply the entry point.

Hidden Layers

Where the "Deep" in Deep Learning lives. These layers learn abstract feature representations.

Output Layer

Produces the final prediction. Activation depends on task (Sigmoid, Softmax, or Linear).

Forward Propagation

Forward propagation is the process of data flowing from input to output to make a prediction.

$a^{(l)} = f(W^{(l)} a^{(l-1)} + b^{(l)})$

The output of layer $(l-1)$ is the input to layer $(l)$.

// PyTorch Conceptual Structure model = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(2, 4), # Input layer (2) to Hidden (4) nn.ReLU(), # Non-linear activation nn.Linear(4, 1), # Hidden (4) to Output (1) nn.Sigmoid() # Binary classification output )

Depth vs Width

Width

Number of neurons in a layer. More width allows learning more features at the same level of abstraction.

Depth

Number of layers. More depth allows for hierarchical learning (e.g., Layer 1: edges, Layer 2: shapes, Layer 3: faces).

XOR Problem Insights

A single neuron cannot solve XOR because the data is not linearly separable. An ANN solves it by using a hidden layer to "bend" the feature space, allowing the output layer to separate the classes with a simple line.

Single Neuron: ❌ Two-Layer ANN: ✅

learning/deep-learning/blocks/block04.title: Loss & Optimization
learning/deep-learning/blocks/block04.description: How does the network know it is wrong, and how does it improve? This block separates those who build models from those who understand training.
learning/deep-learning/blocks/block04.html:
The Learning Loop

A neural network learns by making a prediction, measuring how "wrong" it is via a Loss Function, and then using an Optimizer to adjust weights and reduce that error.

Loss Function

"The Scorecard: Tells us how far we are from the truth."

Optimizer

"The Guide: Tells us how to change weights to improve the score."

Essential Loss Functions

Mean Squared Error (MSE)

Common in Regression. Punishes large errors heavily.

$MSE = \frac{1}{n} \sum (y - \hat{y})^2$

Binary Cross-Entropy (Log Loss)

Standard for Binary Classification. Penalizes confident wrong predictions.

$L = -[y\log(\hat{y}) + (1-y)\log(1-\hat{y})]$

Gradient Descent & Learning Rate

Optimization is like finding the bottom of a valley in the dark. We move weights in the direction that reduces loss: $w = w - \eta \cdot \nabla L$.

The Learning Rate ($\eta$) Strategy:

  • Too Small: Excruciatingly slow convergence.
  • Too Large: Overshooting the minimum, divergence, and chaos.
  • Adam Optimizer: Adaptive step sizes (The Industry Default).

Practice Problems: Block 4

Level 1: Conceptual

1. Loss vs Optimizer

Explain the difference using a real-world analogy (e.g., hiking or exam preparation).

2. Accuracy Trap

Why do we not use accuracy as a loss function during training? (Hint: Think about the gradient).

Level 2: Reasoning

3. Choosing the correct loss

Task: Predict Digit recognition (0-9). Choose the output activation AND the loss function. Explain why.

4. Loss Behavior

Model A and B have the same accuracy, but Model A has lower loss. Which is better and why?

Level 3: Debugging

5. Flat Loss Curve

Your training loss is flat and not decreasing. Give three possible reasons (consider Learning Rate and Data).

learning/deep-learning/blocks/block05.title: Backpropagation
learning/deep-learning/blocks/block05.description: The most important block in Deep Learning. This is how we assign "blame" for an error to millions of weights across the network.
learning/deep-learning/blocks/block05.html:
The Blame Game

Backpropagation answers one critical question: How should each weight change to reduce the loss? It uses the Chain Rule to flow the error backward from the output layer to the input.

"Forward propagation is for data to make predictions. Backward propagation is for error to find responsibility."

$\frac{dL}{dw} = \frac{dL}{dy} \cdot \frac{dy}{dz} \cdot \frac{dz}{dw}$

The Chain Rule: The heart of every neural network training step.

Vanishing & Exploding Gradients

Vanishing

Gradients approach zero. Early layers stop learning. Common with Sigmoid and Tanh because their derivatives are small at extremes.

Exploding

Gradients become excessively large, making training unstable. Common in very deep networks or RNNs.

PyTorch's Autograd

You rarely write the chain rule by hand. PyTorch builds a Computation Graph and applies the chain rule automatically when you call loss.backward().

// One line triggers the whole backward flow # Prediction and loss output = model(input) loss = criterion(output, target) # BACKPROP: Computes dL/dw for every weight in the model loss.backward() # Look inside a weight to see its "responsibility" print(model.layer1.weight.grad)

Mastering Block 5

  • Explain why ReLU prevents vanishing gradients.
  • Describe what .grad represents after a backward pass.
  • Define the difference between Backprop and Optimizer.

learning/deep-learning/blocks/block06.title: Regularization & Generalization
learning/deep-learning/blocks/block06.description:
Deep networks overfit by default. This block teaches
                you how to force models to learn the underlying rule, not just the noise.
learning/deep-learning/blocks/block06.html:
The Overfitting Problem

Overfitting happens when the model is so flexible it "memorizes" the training data, including the noise, causing it to fail on new, unseen data.

Overfitting Signs

Low Training Loss, but High Validation Loss. The model is essentially cheating by looking at the answer key too closely.

Generalization

The true goal of learning. The model captures the underlying pattern (signal), not the specific random fluctuations (noise).

Regularization Techniques

Regularization methods intentionally limit the model's freedom to prevent it from fitting the noise. Think of it as adding "constraints" to keep the model honest.

Dropout

Randomly disables neurons during training. This forces the network to be redundant and robust, as it can't rely on any specific neuron to do all the work.

L2 Regularization (Weight Decay)

Penalizes large weights in the loss function. It prevents the model from relying too heavily on any single feature by keeping weight values small and distributed.

$L_{total} = L_{data} + \lambda \sum w^2$

The Engineer's Monitoring Habit

You cannot manage what you do not measure. Learning happens in the gap between Training and Validation loss. Use these plots to diagnose your model's health.

Learning Pattern Diagnosis
Both Curves Trending Down Learning well (Healthy)
Train Down, Validation Climbing Up Overfitting (Bad)
Both Curves Flat and High Underfitting (Needs more capacity)

Weight Decay in PyTorch

Implementing weight decay is as simple as passing a parameter to your optimizer constructor.

optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), weight_decay=1e-4)

learning/flask/days/day01.html:
The Client-Server Model

The web is simply computers talking to other computers. Your browser (Chrome, Firefox) is the Client, and the computer running your code is the Server.

[Image of client server architecture diagram]

Client

Sends requests. Lives in the browser. Displays the UI (HTML/CSS).

Server (Flask)

Listens for requests. Runs Python logic. Talks to databases.

HTTP Methods (The Verbs)

GET

Fetch data. Safe to call multiple times. Example: Loading your profile page.

POST

Create data. Submitting a form or uploading a file. Example: Registering a user.

PUT

Update data. Replaces existing information. Example: Changing your username.

DELETE

Remove data. Deletes a resource. Example: Deleting a post.

HTTP Request & Response 

// Request Example
GET /profile?id=3 HTTP/1.1
Host: example.com
Content-Type: application/json
// Response Example
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/html
Body: <h1>Welcome!</h1>

Status Codes (The Cheat Sheet)

2xx (Success)

200 OK, 201 Created

3xx (Redirection)

301 Moved, 302 Found

4xx (Client Error)

400 Bad Request, 404 Not Found

5xx (Server Error)

500 Internal Server Error

🍽️ Restaurant Analogy

Think of a web request like ordering food at a restaurant:

  • Customer The Client (Your Browser)
  • Menu The Available Routes (URLs)
  • Chef The Backend Logic (Flask)
  • Waiter The HTTP Protocol (The messenger)

learning/flask/days/day02.html:
Virtual Environments (venv)

Backend development requires isolation. A Virtual Environment is a private box where your project lives alone, preventing version conflicts between different apps.

Setup Commands

# Create the environment
python -m venv venv
# Activate (Windows)
venv\Scripts\activate
# Activate (Mac/Linux)
source venv/bin/activate

Pip & requirements.txt

pip (The Manager)

Installs 3rd-party libraries like Flask.

pip install flask

requirements.txt

A record of every package needed.

Flask==2.3.2
SQLAlchemy==2.0.25

The "Backend Style" Structure

Unlike scripts, backend apps need a organized hierarchy to remain scalable and testable.

project/
app/ # Logic & Routes
├── __init__.py
├── routes.py
└── models.py
├── requirements.txt
├── .env # Secrets
└── run.py

🧪 Day 2 Mission

1. Build Your Box

Create a new folder, initialize a virtual environment, and activate it.

2. Install Flask

Run pip install flask and then create your requirements.txt file using pip freeze > requirements.txt.

Security Rule: Always add venv/ and .env to a .gitignore file. Never share your secrets or your private box with GitHub.

learning/flask/days/day03.title: Flask Internals & Lifecycle
learning/flask/days/day03.description: Understanding how Flask lives, runs, and handles thousands of users without mixing up their data.
learning/flask/days/day03.html:
The Anatomy of Flask(__name__)

Flask needs to know where your files are. By passing __name__, you give Flask a reference point to find your templates and static assets. 

from flask import Flask

app = Flask(__name__) // Tells Flask: "Look for files in this folder"

The Application Lifecycle

It is critical to distinguish between things that happen once and things that happen per request.

Startup Time (Once)

  • • App Object Created
  • • Config & Env Loaded
  • • Routes Registered

Request Time (Per User)

  • • Context Created
  • • View Function Runs
  • • Context Destroyed

Isolation via Contexts

Flask uses "Contexts" to ensure that User A's data never leaks into User B's request. This is why Flask is Thread-Safe.

Application Context

Shared across the whole app. Contains configuration and DB connection settings.

Request Context

Specific to ONE user. Contains headers, form data, and the current session.

⚠️ Backend Rules of Thumb

X

Don't store data in Globals. If you set a global variable for one user, every other user will see it. Use the session object instead.

X

Avoid top-level logic. Code outside of route functions runs exactly once (at startup). It cannot access user data like request.args.

✓

Debug Mode is for Dev only. It provides a stack trace that reveals your source code to hackers. Turn it off in production!

learning/flask/days/day04.title: Routing Deep Dive
learning/flask/days/day04.description: Mastering how Flask maps URLs to logic, ensures security, and builds a scalable API structure.
learning/flask/days/day04.html:
Static vs. Dynamic Routing

Routing is the "Traffic Controller" of your app. Static routes handle fixed pages, while dynamic routes use variables to handle thousands of unique items (like users or posts) with a single function.

Static Route

@app.route('/about')

One URL ➔ One Function

Dynamic Route

@app.route('/user/<id>')

Infinite URLs ➔ One Logic

URL Converters (Type Safety)

Converters are your first line of defense. They prevent the function from running if the data type is wrong.

Converter Matches Example
<int:id> Integers only /user/5
<float:val> Decimals /price/19.99
<uuid:pub> Unique IDs /v1/78e...

Dynamic URL Building

Rule: Never hardcode your URLs. If you change a route path in Python, url_for() automatically updates every link in your app.

<a href="/login"> Fragile & Bad
url_for('login') Scalable & Good

🧠 The RESTful Mindset

Instead of creating dozens of URLs like /delete_user, use HTTP methods to keep your routing clean and logical.

GET /users
List all users
POST /users
Create new user
DELETE /users/<id>
Remove a user

learning/flask/days/day05.title: Request & Response
learning/flask/days/day05.description: Translating raw HTTP traffic into clean Python objects and professional server responses.
learning/flask/days/day05.html:
The request Object

Flask wraps every detail the client sends—URLs, headers, and data—into a single global-like object called request. This object is isolated per user through the Request Context.

The Data Map (Where to find what)

request.args URL Query Params (?q=flask)
request.form HTML Form Data (POST)
request.json API / JSON Payloads

Metadata: Headers & Cookies

Headers

The "Instructions." They carry metadata like Content-Type or Authorization tokens.

Cookies

The "Memory." Stored in the browser to maintain state (like sessions) across independent requests.

Professional Responses

A response tells the client exactly what happened using a Status Code and provides the Body (HTML/JSON).

Common Status Codes
200 OK (Success)
201 Created (Success)
400 Bad Request (Client Error)
404 Not Found (Client Error)
500 Server Error (Backend Bug)

🧪 Day 5 Challenge

Backend rule: Never trust the client. Use the .get() method to handle missing data gracefully.

# Prevents KeyError if 'id' is missing
user_id = request.args.get('id')
page = request.args.get('page', 1)

learning/flask/days/day06.title: Templates & Jinja2
learning/flask/days/day06.description: Mastering Server-Side Rendering (SSR) to build dynamic, secure, and maintainable user interfaces.
learning/flask/days/day06.html:
Server-Side Rendering (SSR)

In Flask, HTML is generated on the Server before being sent to the browser. This ensures fast initial loads and excellent SEO.

The Logic (Python)

return render_template('index.html', user=u)

The UI (Jinja2)

<h1>Hello {{ user.name }}</h1>

The DRY Principle: Inheritance

Instead of copy-pasting your navbar and footer, use Template Inheritance to create a base layout that other pages simply "fill in."

# base.html (The Parent)
<nav>...</nav>
{% block content %}{% endblock %}
<footer>...</footer>
# home.html (The Child)
{% extends "base.html" %}
{% block content %}
<h1>Welcome to Home</h1>
{% endblock %}

Loops & Conditions

Conditional Logic

{% if user.is_active %}
  <span>Online</span>
{% else %}
  <span>Offline</span>
{% endif %}

Dynamic Lists

{% for item in items %}
  <li>{{ item.name }}</li>
{% endfor %}

🔒 Auto-Escaping Security

Jinja2 automatically prevents Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) by turning dangerous characters into harmless text. This is a core backend safety feature.

User Input
<script>alert('Hacked')</script>
Rendered Output
<script>...

learning/flask/days/day07.title: Static Files & Project Structure
learning/flask/days/day07.description: Mastering asset management and professional software organization to build scalable applications.
learning/flask/days/day07.html:
What are Static Files?

Static files are assets that do not change per user and are served "as-is" by the server. Unlike templates, the backend performs zero processing on these files.

CSS (Styles)
JS (Logic)
Images/Icons

Key Rule: Assets vs Templates

Templates are dynamic (rendered per request). Static files are fixed and cached by browsers to improve speed and reduce server load.

The Purpose of the /static Folder

Flask enforces a specific static/ directory to ensure:

  • Security: Prevents users from accessing arbitrary backend files (like your database or .env).
  • MIME Types: Automatically tells the browser if a file is an image, script, or style.
  • Organization: Provides a predictable URL structure: /static/style.css.

Professional Project Structure

Stop putting everything in one file. Real software engineering requires modularity.

project/
├── app/
├── __init__.py # Turns folder into a package
├── routes/ # Handlers
├── models/ # DB Logic
static/ # Global Assets
templates/ # HTML Files
├── migrations/
├── venv/ # (DO NOT GIT COMMIT)
├── requirements.txt
└── run.py

Separation of Concerns

Part Responsibility
Routes Handle URLs & Requests
Models Database logic & Data rules
Templates UI & Presentation (HTML)
Static Assets (CSS/JS/Images)
Config Environment Settings & API Keys

Rules & Security

Avoid These

  • Inline CSS/JS inside templates
  • Committing venv/ to Git
  • Serving user uploads directly from static/
  • Using random filenames (be descriptive!)

Do These

  • Keep static files in Version Control
  • Structure templates to mirror routes
  • Use external CSS for browser caching
  • Structure early to avoid "technical debt"

Day 7 Outcome

You have completed the foundation week. You are now ready for Week 2: Databases & Logic. You should now be able to:

  • Organize a modular Flask app
  • Efficiently link CSS & JS
  • Handle static asset security
  • Implement Separation of Concerns

learning/flask/days/day08.title: Forms & User Input
learning/flask/days/day08.description: Mastering the flow of data from browser to server while implementing industry-standard security and validation.
learning/flask/days/day08.html:
The Golden Rule: Never Trust the Browser

Every piece of user input is untrusted. Malicious users can bypass your HTML, modify your JavaScript, or use tools like curl to send fake requests.

Backend Mindset:

Always assume form data is wrong, missing, or tampered with until it is proven valid by the server.

The Form Submission Flow

1. User fills form & Submits

Browser sends a POST request with encoded data.

2. Flask receives request

Data is stored in request.form as raw strings.

3. Server-Side Validation (The Gatekeeper)

Flask-WTF checks for length, format, and security tokens.

4. Action & Response

Data is saved to DB, and the user is redirected or shown errors.

Client-Side vs Server-Side

Client-Side (HTML/JS)

User Experience Only

Immediate feedback for users. Prevents accidental empty submissions.

BYPASSABLE
Server-Side (Flask)

Security Mandatory

Cannot be bypassed. Protects your database and business logic.

NON-NEGOTIABLE

CRITICAL: CSRF Protection

Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF) is an attack where a user is tricked into performing actions on your site without their consent while they are logged in.

How it attacks?

It exploits the browser's behavior of automatically sending cookies with requests.

How we stop it?

Flask-WTF injects a unique, random CSRF Token that must match on every POST request.

Common Beginner Mistakes

  • Trusting frontend validation as your only line of defense.
  • Saving data to the database before running form.validate_on_submit().
  • Failing silently instead of showing specific errors to the user.

Day 8 Checkpoint

  • Understand why request.form is untrusted
  • Explain the role of Flask-WTF as a safety layer
  • Define CSRF and how tokens prevent it
  • Realize that validation is part of UX and Security

learning/flask/days/day09.title: Database Theory
learning/flask/days/day09.description: The blueprint of the backend. Understanding how data survives, connects, and stays consistent.
learning/flask/days/day09.html:
Memory vs. Persistence

RAM (Memory)

  • • Fast, but temporary
  • • Lost on server restart
  • • Where Python variables live

Database (Disk)

  • • Persistent and shared
  • • Survives restarts & crashes
  • • Structured for fast access

The Core Structure

Think of a Database as a collection of Excel sheets, but with strict rules.

Table: Users

1
alice_dev
alice@mail.com

2
bob_coder
bob@mail.com

Table

The "Thing" (Class)

Row

One Record (Object)

Column

Attribute (Field)

Relationships & Keys

Primary Key (PK)

The unique passport for every row. It must never change and never repeat.

Foreign Key (FK)

A column that points to the Primary Key of another table. This is how we link a Post to its Author.

The CRUD Operations

Operation Database Action
Create Adding a new row (Signup, New Post)
Read Fetching data (Profile page, Feed)
Update Modifying a row (Edit Profile, Change Password)
Delete Removing data (Delete Account, Remove Comment)

Day 9 Outcome

Before writing code, you must master the "Think before you store" mindset. You should now be able to:

  • Differentiate RAM vs. Disk storage
  • Map real-world items to Tables/Rows
  • Explain why PKs are mandatory
  • Understand SQL vs. NoSQL basics

learning/flask/days/day10.title: SQLAlchemy ORM
learning/flask/days/day10.description: Bridging the gap between Python Objects and Relational Databases.
learning/flask/days/day10.html:
The Core Problem: Language Mismatch

Databases speak SQL (Relational). Python speaks Objects. Without a bridge, you have to write messy SQL strings inside your Python code.

Manual Way (Hard)

"INSERT INTO users (name) VALUES ('" + name + "')"

ORM Way (Smart)

user = User(name="Alice")

Mapping Tables to Classes

Database (SQL) Python (SQLAlchemy)
Table Class
Row Object Instance
Column Attribute
Primary Key Object ID

The Session: The Gatekeeper

SQLAlchemy doesn't save data immediately. It uses a Session to track changes. Think of it as a "drafting area."

1

Add to Session

"I want to save this object later."

2

Commit Transaction

"Write all my changes to the disk now."

Backend Rule: Nothing is saved automatically. If you don't commit, your data is lost when the request ends.

Thinking in Objects

Queries

Instead of SQL SELECT, you ask the Class:
"User, give me the person with ID 5."

Relationships

Instead of manual joins, you access attributes:
"user.posts" gives you their articles automatically.

Day 10 Outcome

You are now ready to write Python code that controls a database. You should be able to:

  • Explain the Class ↔ Table relationship
  • Define the role of a Session in transaction safety
  • Understand why ORMs prevent SQL Injection
  • Distinguish between a Model (blueprint) and Instance (data)

learning/flask/days/day11.title: Database Migrations
learning/flask/days/day11.description: Version control for your data structure. Learn to evolve your database without losing user data.
learning/flask/days/day11.html:
Why Schema Changes Are Dangerous

A Schema is the blueprint of your database (tables, columns, types). When you change your code (e.g., adding a "bio" column to a User), the database doesn't magically update.

The Production Risk

In production, you can't just delete the database and start over. Real users have real data. If you change a data type incorrectly, you could corrupt or lose every record in that table.

Migrations = Version Control

Think of migrations as Git for your database structure. Each migration is a "commit" that tracks a specific change.

VERSION 1

ID, Username, Password

VERSION 2

+ Added Email column

VERSION 3

+ Renamed Password to Hash

Recreating vs. Migrating

Recreating (❌)

Deletes all existing data. Breaks foreign key references. Fine for local demos, fatal for real apps.

Migrating (✅)

Preserves data. Applies changes incrementally. Can be reviewed and shared with teammates.

The Migration Workflow 

Upgrade
Moves the schema forward. (e.g., Adding a 'created_at' timestamp).


Downgrade
Reverses a change. (Warning: some changes, like deleting a column, are harder to reverse safely).

Common Beginner Mistakes

  • Assuming db.create_all() handles future changes. (It only creates missing tables).
  • Deleting migration files manually to "clean up" the project.
  • Applying migrations in production without a database backup.

Day 11 Checkpoint

You have shifted from a "local coder" to a "backend engineer." You should now understand:

  • What a Database Schema is
  • Why migrations protect user data
  • The role of Flask-Migrate
  • The Upgrade/Downgrade cycle

learning/flask/days/day12.title: CRUD Patterns
learning/flask/days/day12.description: Mastering the fundamental operations of every backend application: Create, Read, Update, and Delete.
learning/flask/days/day12.html:
The CRUD/HTTP Mapping

CRUD is a design pattern that describes how data flows between the user and the database. Professionally, we map these actions to specific HTTP Methods.

Action HTTP Flask Logic
Create POST Add new resource
Read GET Fetch resource(s)
Update PUT/PATCH Modify existing data
Delete DELETE Remove resource

Creation & Validation Lifecycle

Validate First

Creation or updates should never happen without re-validating the data on the server.

Commit Transaction

Use SQLAlchemy sessions to ensure the data is written permanently.

The Update Rule

Never assume existing data is correct. When updating, ensure you aren't accidentally overwriting fields the user didn't intend to change.

Delete: The Dangerous Operation

Hard Delete

Permanently removes the row from the database. Irreversible and can break relationships (e.g., deleting a user but leaving their posts).

Soft Delete (Professional Choice)

Instead of deleting, we set a is_deleted flag to True. The data stays in the DB but is hidden from the UI. Safer and allows for "Undo" functionality.

Pagination & Security

Pagination

Never load an entire table. As your app grows, fetching 10,000 rows will crash your server. Design for small chunks (e.g., 20 items at a time).

Ownership

CRUD is a security boundary. Always check: "Does this user own the resource they are trying to Update or Delete?"

Day 12 Outcome

You have mastered the data-flow patterns used by professional backends. You should now be able to:

  • Map CRUD to HTTP Methods
  • Explain why Delete is a business decision
  • Design routes for single vs multiple resources
  • Understand the need for Pagination

learning/flask/days/day13.title: Application Architecture
learning/flask/days/day13.description: Scaling Flask from a single script to a professional, maintainable codebase.
learning/flask/days/day13.html:
The Application Factory

Instead of a global app object, we use a function to create the app instance. This allows for easier testing and multiple configurations. 

def create_app(config_class=Config):
app = Flask(__name__)
app.config.from_object(config_class)
# Initialize extensions
db.init_app(app)
migrate.init_app(app, db)
return app

Blueprints: Modular Routing

Blueprints allow you to organize your application into distinct components, such as auth, main, and api.

Structure

Group related routes, templates, and static files into independent folders.

Reusability

Easily plug features in and out of different projects.

Day 13 Outcome

You are now thinking like a software architect. You should be able to:

  • Convert a single-file app into a Factory pattern
  • Register Blueprints for different modules
  • Organize folder structures for large projects

learning/flask/days/day14.title: Mini Project 1: Putting it Together
learning/flask/days/day14.description: The transition from learning concepts to building systems. Plan, design, and execute your first real-world Flask application.
learning/flask/days/day14.html:
The Backend Developer Workflow

Step 1: Define Entities

Decide what data objects exist (e.g., Users, Notes, Tasks).

Step 2: Schema Design

Design tables and relationships (Day 9 theory).

Step 3: Route Mapping

Plan your URLs and HTTP methods for each action.

Think in Features

"Create a Note" is a feature. "Insert row into DB" is the technical implementation. Always start with the feature.

The Data Blueprint

Before coding, sketch your relationship. This prevents circular imports and migration nightmares later.

User Model

  • id (PK)
  • username (Unique)
  • password (Hashed)

Note Model

  • id (PK)
  • title
  • content
  • user_id (FK)

Mapping Features to CRUD

Feature URL CRUD / HTTP
Add Note /notes/new Create (POST)
Browse Notes /notes Read (GET)
Edit Note /notes/<id>/edit Update (POST)
Remove Note /notes/<id>/delete Delete (POST)

The Architecture Audit

Even for a mini-project, follow professional standards. Does your app use:

  • Blueprints

    Separate routes for 'auth' and 'notes' into modules.

  • App Factory

    Using create_app() to prevent circular imports.

  • CSRF & Validation

    Protecting every POST request with Flask-WTF tokens.

Milestone Reached!

You are no longer "just learning." You are now building backend systems. Completion of Day 14 marks your transition from student to developer.

Foundations Complete Ready for Week 3

learning/flask/days/day15.title: Authentication Theory
learning/flask/days/day15.description: Mastering identity. Learn how to securely recognize users in a stateless web environment.
learning/flask/days/day15.html:
The Hashing Gold Standard

Passwords must never be stored in plain text or encrypted. They must be hashed. Hashing is a one-way cryptographic function that protects user data even if your database is stolen.

Hashing (One-Way)

Input "123" becomes "$2b$12$Kjs...". There is no way to turn that hash back into "123".

Encryption (Two-Way)

Can be reversed with a key. Never use this for passwords because keys can be leaked.

The Authentication Flow 

User submits Password
Server hashes input + Salt
Compare against stored Hash

Sessions vs. Tokens

Feature Sessions (Cookies) Tokens (JWT)
Storage Server-side Memory/DB Stateless (Client-only)
Scaling Harder (Needs shared DB) Easier (No DB lookup)
Best Use Standard Web Apps Mobile & APIs

The Fatal Five Mistakes

  • Storing any secret (like a real password) in a cookie.
  • Rolling your own hashing algorithm. (Use Bcrypt or Argon2).
  • Forgetting to Salt your hashes.
  • Mixing Auth (Identity) with Authorization (Permissions).

Day 15 Outcome

You now understand the infrastructure of identity. Before moving to Day 16, ensure you can:

  • Explain why HTTP is "stateless"
  • Describe the 1-way nature of hashing
  • Define a Session vs a Cookie
  • Explain why Auth bugs are critical

learning/flask/days/day16.title: 🧠 User Authentication in Flask
learning/flask/days/day16.description: Mastering identity, session management, and access control without breaking security.
learning/flask/days/day16.html:
The Three Pillars of Auth

User Model

The single source of truth for identity.

Session Mgmt

How the server "remembers" who you are.

Route Protection

Restricting access to private data.

The Login Flow & Persistence

Being "logged in" means the browser sends an identifier (cookie) that Flask maps to a database user on every single request.

[Image of web authentication login flow diagram]
1
User submits form → Server verifies Hash vs Database
2
If match: session['user_id'] = user.id
3
Browser receives & stores encrypted Session Cookie

The Request Lifecycle

Every Request Lifecycle

1. Flask reads Session Cookie
2. Extract user_id
3. User Loader: User.query.get(id)
4. Attach user to request context (current_user)

This ensures auth state is thread-safe and isolated per user session.

✅ Day 16 Checkpoint

Before moving to Day 17, ensure you can:

  • Explain why the "User Loader" function is necessary
  • Describe the flow from Login Form to Session Cookie
  • Explain the security importance of the Logout process
  • Identify the difference between Authentication and Authorization

learning/flask/days/day17.title: Authorization & Roles
learning/flask/days/day17.description: Mastering access control: the "What can you do?" of backend engineering.
learning/flask/days/day17.html:
Authentication vs. Authorization

It is a common mistake to think that because a user is "Logged In," they have permission to do everything. In professional backends, we treat these as two entirely separate gates.

Authentication

"Who are you?" (Passport/Login)

Authorization

"What can you do?" (Clearance/Permissions)

The 3 Core Questions

Every time a user tries to access a page or modify data, the backend must pass three sequential tests:

Step 1

Is the user logged in? (Authentication)

Step 2

Does the user have the right role? (Admin vs. User)

Step 3

Does the user own this data? (Ownership)

Roles vs. Permissions

Model Context Example
Roles High-level categories admin, editor, viewer
Permissions Specific granular actions can_delete_user, can_edit_post

Critical Threat: Privilege Escalation

This happens when a normal user finds a way to perform admin actions. Usually because the developer checked the "Login" status but forgot to check the "Role" or "Ownership."

Backend Secret: "Deny by Default." If you don't explicitly grant a user permission to do something, the server should say no. Never allow access unless proven otherwise.

learning/flask/days/day18.title: REST API Design
learning/flask/days/day18.description: Learning the "Architecture of the Internet." Design professional APIs that are stateless, scalable, and easy to consume.
learning/flask/days/day18.html:
Resources, Not Actions

In REST, the URL should always identify a Noun (the thing), never a Verb (the action). You use the HTTP Method to describe the action.

❌ Action-Based (Bad)

/getUser/5
/deletePost/12
/createComment

✅ Resource-Based (REST)

/users/5
/posts/12
/comments

The Vocabulary of HTTP

REST leverages the existing architecture of the web. By using standard methods, any client (mobile app, browser, or server) knows exactly what to expect.

Method Database (CRUD) Intent
GET Read Fetch a resource
POST Create Add a new resource
PATCH Update Modify a resource
DELETE Delete Remove a resource

Statelessness: The Key to Scale

A REST API is Stateless. The server does not store "sessions." Every request from the client must contain all the information necessary to understand and authorize that request (usually via a Token).

"Statelessness allows us to spin up 100 servers, and a request can go to any one of them and still work."

The API's Language

In REST, we use status codes to communicate result states. An API should never return a "200 OK" if the actual result was an error.

201 Created

Returned after a successful POST request.

403 Forbidden

User is authenticated but lacks permission.

learning/flask/days/day19.title: Building REST APIs
learning/flask/days/day19.description: Trading HTML templates for JSON data. Learn how to turn your Flask app into a powerful data service for mobile and web apps.
learning/flask/days/day19.html:
The Format Shift

In a traditional web app, the server returns a fully rendered HTML page. In an API, the server returns JSON—a raw data format that the client (React, iOS, Android) uses to build its own UI.

HTML Output

<h1>User: Parsa</h1>

JSON Output

{ "username": "parsa" }

The API Request Lifecycle

When a client calls an API, the Flask process changes slightly. Instead of parsing form fields, it parses JSON bodies; instead of rendering templates, it Serializes data.

Serialization Converting complex DB objects into plain JSON strings.
Validation Checking that incoming JSON has the right structure and types.

APIs are Promises

The Contract Mindset

Unlike a website where you can change the UI anytime, an API response is a "Contract." If you change a field name, you break the mobile apps and services that rely on you. This is why Versioning (e.g., /v1/) is mandatory.

Status Codes are the UI

In APIs, there are no error pages. The HTTP Status Code is the only way the client knows what happened.

201 Created Success (POST)
422 Unprocessable Validation Error
401 Unauthorized Token Required
403 Forbidden No Permission

learning/flask/days/day20.title: API Auth & JWT
learning/flask/days/day20.description: Moving beyond sessions to stateless, token-based security for scalable modern backends.
learning/flask/days/day20.html:
The Shift to Token-Based Auth

Unlike web apps that use cookies and sessions (stateful), APIs must be Stateless. The server shouldn't remember the client; instead, the client presents a "digital passport"—a Token—with every request.

Sessions (Stateful)

Stored in server memory or DB. Hard to scale across multiple servers.

JWT (Stateless)

Self-contained info. Verified instantly by any server instance using a secret key.

Anatomy of a JWT

A JSON Web Token consists of three parts separated by dots. It is Encoded, not encrypted, meaning anyone can read the data, but only the server can verify it wasn't tampered with.

header. # Algorithm & Token Type
payload. # User ID, Expiry, Roles
signature # The Cryptographic Proof

The Authentication Cycle

1

Login & Issue

Client sends credentials; Server returns a signed JWT.

2

Bearer Token Header

Client attaches Authorization: Bearer <token> to all requests.

3

Verify & Authorize

Server validates the signature and grants access based on payload data.

Refresh Token Strategy

Since JWTs are stateless, you cannot easily "revoke" them. We use short-lived Access Tokens (15 min) and long-lived Refresh Tokens to keep users logged in securely.

Security Alert: Never store sensitive data (passwords, social security numbers) in a JWT payload. It is Base64 encoded and easily readable by anyone.

learning/flask/days/day21.title: Mini Project 2: Secure REST API
learning/flask/days/day21.description: Architecting a production-style backend. This is where JWT, REST, and Ownership Logic meet.
learning/flask/days/day21.html:
Defining the Resource

In API development, we don't think in pages; we think in Resources. For this project, a "Note" is a resource that belongs to a specific user.

# The Resource Schema (JSON)
{
"id": 101,
"title": "Secure Backend",
"owner_id": 5,
"created_at": "2026-01-07"
}

The Endpoint Map

Method Endpoint Auth
POST /auth/login Public
GET /notes JWT Required
PATCH /notes/<id> Owner Only
DELETE /notes/<id> Owner Only

Enforcing Ownership

It’s not enough to be logged in. Your API must verify that User A cannot edit User B’s data. This logic happens at the view level.

Security Checklist

  • • Is the token valid and not expired?
  • • Does the resource ID exist in the database?
  • • Does the resource's owner_id match the JWT sub?

Project Deliverable

By the end of this day, your backend should be a pure Data Service. No HTML, no flashes—just precise JSON and status codes.

Success Response
200 OK + { "data": [...] }
Auth Error
401 Unauthorized + { "err": "..." }

learning/flask/days/day22.title: 🧠 Error Handling & Logging
learning/flask/days/day22.description: The difference between a student and an engineer: Building systems that bend but don't break.
learning/flask/days/day22.html:
The Anatomy of Failure

Errors are inevitable. Your job isn't to prevent every error—it's to handle them without crashing the entire system.

Client Errors (User's Fault)

Invalid input, expired tokens, missing resources.

400 Bad Request 404 Not Found

Server Errors (Our Fault)

Bugs, DB downtime, unhandled exceptions.

500 Internal Error 503 Service Unavailable

Graceful Failure vs. Hard Crash

❌ The Crash

Traceback (most recent call last):
File "app.py", line 42, in index
ZeroDivisionError: division by zero

Leaks internal code and stops the server.

✅ The Airbag

HTTP/1.1 500 Internal Error
Content-Type: application/json

{"error": "Internal server error"}

Protects data, hides logic, and stays online.

Production Logging: The Black Box

In production, you don't have a debugger. Your logs are your only visibility into what happened.

DEBUG

Granular info for dev (DB queries, variable states)

INFO

Normal operations (User login, payment processed)

WARNING

Something unusual but not a failure yet (Low disk space)

ERROR

Operation failed (External API timeout, DB error)

Backend Security Rules

  • I. Never log passwords, credit cards, or auth tokens.
  • II. Never show raw stack traces to users.
  • III. If a process matters, log its start, its failure, and its success.

✅ Day 22 Outcome

Before moving to Day 23, ensure you can:

  • Differentiate between Client (4xx) and Server (5xx) errors
  • Explain why logging beats print() in production
  • List three things that should never be present in a log file
  • Describe the concept of "Graceful Failure"

learning/flask/days/day24.title: JSON & REST APIs
learning/flask/days/day24.description: Bridging the gap between Go data structures and the web. Master the encoding and decoding of JSON to build modern APIs.
learning/flask/days/day24.html:
JSON Mapping & Struct Tags

Go uses "struct tags" to control how field names appear in JSON output. Fields must be exported (Capitalized) for the JSON package to see them.

type Student struct {
    ID   int     `json:"id"`
    Name string  `json:"name"`
    GPA  float64 `json:"gpa"`
}

Encoding & Decoding

Marshal (Struct → JSON)

Converting a Go object into a JSON byte slice.

jsonData, _ := json.Marshal(student)

Unmarshal (JSON → Struct)

Parsing JSON bytes back into a Go struct.

json.Unmarshal(data, &student)

The API Handler Pattern

When building APIs, we use Encoders and Decoders to stream JSON directly from the request and response bodies.

// Sending JSON
w.Header().Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
json.NewEncoder(w).Encode(student)

// Receiving JSON
json.NewDecoder(r.Body).Decode(&s)

🧪 Mini Exercises

01

Create a /students endpoint that returns a hardcoded slice of student structs as a JSON array.

02

Create a POST endpoint that accepts a student JSON object, decodes it into a struct, and prints it to the terminal.

Think: Why does Go require fields to be capitalized (exported) for the json package to work? (Answer: The JSON package uses reflection to inspect the struct; reflection cannot access private/unexported fields.)

learning/flask/days/day25.title: Environment & Config
learning/flask/days/day25.description: Decoupling code from configuration. Learn how to manage secrets and settings safely across different environments.
learning/flask/days/day25.html:
Why Environment Variables?

Environment variables are key–value pairs provided by the OS. They are critical for keeping Secrets (API keys) and Configuration (Database hosts) out of your source code.

❌ Bad Practice

const apiKey = "SECRET_123"

✅ Good Practice

key := os.Getenv("API_KEY")

Implementation in Go

Go's os package makes it simple. If a variable doesn't exist, it returns an empty string.

// Get value
port := os.Getenv("PORT")
// Handle default
if port == "" {
    port = "8080"
}

The .env File Pattern

Local Development

In real-world projects, we use a .env file. Never commit this to Git.

PORT=8080
DB_NAME=students_db
DEBUG=true

🧪 Mini Exercises

01

Write a program that attempts to read an environment variable called APP_NAME and prints it to the console.

02

Update your REST server to read the PORT from the environment, defaulting to 8080 if not set.

Think: Why is it dangerous to store even "minor" API keys in a public GitHub repository? (Answer: Because automated scrapers constantly scan GitHub for keys to exploit services, and once committed, a key is permanently in the Git history.)

learning/flask/days/day26.title: Go Best Practices
learning/flask/days/day26.description: Writing "idiomatic" Go. Learn the conventions and philosophy that separate a Go developer from someone just writing C++ or Java in Go.
learning/flask/days/day26.html:
The Zen of Go

Go values simplicity and readability over "clever" code. If a junior developer can't understand your logic at first glance, it likely isn't idiomatic Go.

  • Explicit over implicit
  • Avoid deep nesting

Standard Layout

For scalable applications, follow the community-accepted folder structure to separate entry points from internal logic.

/cmd // Main applications (binaries)
/internal // Private code; cannot be imported by others
/pkg // Reusable library code
/api // API protocol definitions (Swagger, etc.)

The Mandatory Toolkit

gofmt

Go code has one standard format. Run gofmt -w . to auto-format everything. There are no arguments about curly brace placement in Go.

go vet

Analyzes source code and reports suspicious constructs, such as printf calls whose arguments do not align with the format string.

🧠 Mental Check

01

Review your Student Management System. Are your functions starting with Capital letters unless they need to be private? Idiom: Export only what is necessary.

02

Do you have panic in your handlers? Replace them with return err and handle the failure at the caller level.

Think: Why is it common to see single-letter variable names like r for request or w for writer in Go? (Answer: Go prefers short names for variables with short scopes. If a variable is only used in a 3-line function, its meaning is clear from context.)

learning/flask/days/day27.title: Final Project: Part 1
learning/flask/days/day27.description: Taking everything you've learned to build a professional-grade Student REST API with a multi-layered architecture.
learning/flask/days/day27.html:
Professional Project Structure

Following the "Clean Architecture" principles, we separate our project into layers: the Entry Point, the Domain Models, the Business Logic, and the Web Handlers.

student-api/

├── cmd/server/main.go (App entry point)
└── internal/student/

├── model.go (Data structures)
├── service.go (Business logic)
└── handler.go (HTTP endpoints)

Core Implementation

Service Layer (The "Brain")

This layer handles validation and data persistence, staying independent of the HTTP protocol.

func Validate(s Student) error {
    if s.GPA < 0 || s.GPA > 9 {
        return errors.New("invalid GPA")
    }
    return nil
    }

Handler Layer (The "Mouth")

Translates HTTP requests into data the service understands, and formats service results back into JSON.

json.NewDecoder(r.Body).Decode(&s)
w.Header().Set("Content-Type", "application/json")

Testing Your Progress

cURL Test (Create Student)

curl -X POST http://localhost:8080/students -d '{"name": "Parsa", "gpa": 7.75}' -H "Content-Type: application/json"

🧠 Mid-Project Review

Self-Reflection: Why did we use internal/ for the student package instead of putting it in the root? (Answer: To enforce encapsulation. The "internal" directory is a special Go convention that prevents other modules from importing that code, ensuring it stays private to your application.)

learning/flask/days/day28.title: Final CRUD Implementation
learning/flask/days/day28.description: Completing the Student API: Implementing retrieval, updates, and deletions.
learning/flask/days/day28.html:
Service Logic (CRUD) 

func GetByID(id int) (Student, error) {
    for _, s := range students {
        if s.ID == id { return s, nil }
    }
    return Student{}, errors.New("not found")
}

func UpdateGPA(id int, gpa float64) error {
    for i := range students {
        if students[i].ID == id { students[i].GPA = gpa; return nil }
    }
    return errors.New("not found")
}

func Delete(id int) error {
    // Remove element by re-slicing
    students = append(students[:i], students[i+1:]...)
}

Dynamic ID Routing

Handling paths like /students/{id} by trimming the URL prefix.

idStr := strings.TrimPrefix(r.URL.Path, "/students/")
id, _ := strconv.Atoi(idStr)

Project Checklist

GET /students (All)
GET /students/1 (ID)
POST /students (Create)
DELETE /students/1 (Delete)

learning/github/levels/level1.title: The Foundation
learning/github/levels/level1.description: Understanding the core difference between Git and GitHub, and setting up your first repository.
learning/github/levels/level1.html:
The Big Picture

Git

A "Time Machine" on your computer. It saves versions of your files locally. You don't need internet to use it.

GitHub

A "Cloud Storage" (like Google Drive) for your Git history. It lets you share your work with others online.

First-Time Setup

Before you can save anything, you must introduce yourself to Git. Open your terminal and run these once:

git config --global user.name "Your Name"
git config --global user.email "your.email@example.com"

Starting a Local Web Project

  1. Create a folder: 
    mkdir MyWebProject
cd MyWebProject
  2. Initialize Git: (Tells Git to watch this folder) 
    git init

    You will see "Initialized empty Git repository".

  3. Create your HTML file: 
    <h1>Hello World</h1>
<p>This is my first Git project!</p>

The Saving Workflow (Loop)

1. Check Status

See what Git sees. New files will be red.

git status

2. Stage (Add)

Move file to the "Waiting Room".

git add index.html

3. Commit (Save)

Take a permanent snapshot.

git commit -m "Created homepage"

Connecting to GitHub

  1. Go to github.com and create a New Repository named MyWebProject.
  2. Important: Keep "Add a README" unchecked.
  3. Copy the URL (e.g., https://github.com/User/Repo.git).
  4. Link your terminal: 
    git remote add origin <PASTE-URL-HERE>
  5. Rename Branch & Push: 
    git branch -M main
git push -u origin main

    The -u flag stands for "Upstream". It links your local branch to the GitHub one so you can just type git push later.

Mastery Notes: Cheat Sheet

1. Setup (One time only)

git config --global user.name "My Name"
git config --global user.email "me@example.com"

2. The Loop

git status // Check changes
git add . // Stage ALL files
git commit -m "Message" // Save snapshot

3. Uploading

git push // Uploads code

learning/github/levels/level2.title: Branching & Merging
learning/github/levels/level2.description: Mastering parallel universes. Experiment safely without breaking your main code.
learning/github/levels/level2.html:
The Concept

Imagine you are building a house (your code). You want to see if a new balcony looks good, but you don't want to actually smash a hole in your perfectly good wall just to test it.

In Git, you create a Branch. This creates a "Parallel Universe" copy of your code.

Main Branch

The "Real World" (Keep this safe and working).

Feature Branch

The "Experiment" (Do whatever you want here; if it breaks, who cares?).

Creating a Branch (The Experiment)

Let's add a blue button to your website, but do it safely on a separate branch.

  1. Create and Switch to a new branch:

    We will use the modern command switch -c (Create and Switch).

    git switch -c feature-blue-button

    Your terminal should now say you are on branch 'feature-blue-button'.

  2. Modify your code:

    Open your index.html file. It should look just like it did before. Add a button code:

    <h1>Hello World</h1>
<p>This is my first Git project!</p>
<button style="background-color: blue; color: white;">I am a Blue Button</button>
  3. Save (Commit) to this branch: 
    git add index.html
git commit -m "Added a blue button"

The "Magic" Switch

This is the moment that confuses beginners until they see it happen.

1. Switch back to Main:

Go back to your original timeline.

git switch main

2. Look at your file:

Open index.html (or look at it in your browser). The button is gone!
Git instantly reverted your files to how they look in the main universe. Your work isn't lost; it's just safely stored in the other branch.

Merging (Bringing it Home)

[Image of git merge diagram]

You decided the blue button looks great. Let's bring that change into the main "Real World."

  1. Stay on Main: (Ensure you are on the branch you want to receive the changes). 
    git status

    Should say "On branch main"

  2. Merge: (Absorb the history of the other branch). 
    git merge feature-blue-button

    Open your index.html file now. The button has magically appeared in Main!

Ignoring Junk (.gitignore)

Sometimes you have files you never want to save to Git (e.g., hidden system files, passwords, or huge video files).

  1. Create a file named .gitignore:

    Create this file in your main folder.

  2. Add rules to it:

    Open .gitignore in your editor and type the names of files to ignore. Let's pretend we have a secret file.

    secret-passwords.txt
*.log
  3. Test it:

    Create a file called secret-passwords.txt. Now run:

    git status

    Git will NOT list secret-passwords.txt as a new file. It is invisible to Git.

The Emergency Pause Button (Stash)

[Image of git stash diagram]

Imagine you are working on a "Red Button" branch. You have half-finished code that is broken. Suddenly, your boss says, "Fix a typo on Main right now!"

You can't switch branches because your current code is messy. You need to "Stash" it (put it in a drawer).

1. Stash your changes
git stash
Your folder is now clean (reverted to the last commit), and your messy work is saved in a temporary memory slot.

2. Do your other work...

3. Bring the work back
git stash pop
Your messy work reappears exactly as you left it.

Mastery Notes: Cheat Sheet

1. Branching (Parallel Universes)

git switch -c <name> // Create & Switch
git switch main // Return to original code
git branch // See all branches

2. Merging (Combining)

git switch main // 1. Go to destination
git merge <name> // 2. Absorb changes

3. Ignoring Files

  • Create file .gitignore
  • List file names or patterns (like *.log) inside.
  • Purpose: Keeps the repo clean and secure.

4. Stashing

git stash // Save messy work
git stash pop // Restore work

learning/github/levels/level3.title: The Collaborator
learning/github/levels/level3.description: Working with teams, mastering the Pull Request, and resolving the dreaded Merge Conflict.
learning/github/levels/level3.html:
The Team Workflow Concepts

Clone

"Download" an entire project from the cloud to your computer for the first time.

Pull

"Update" your computer with the changes your teammates pushed to the cloud.

PR

"Asking permission." You don't just shove code into the main codebase; you ask the team to review it first.

The Simulation (Let's Break Things)

We are going to simulate a situation where you and a "teammate" edit the same file at the same time.

Step 1: The Teammate (Edit on GitHub)

Go to GitHub.com, edit index.html, and commit this change:

<h1>Welcome to the BEST Website</h1>

Step 2: You (Edit Locally)

Do NOT pull yet. Edit index.html on your computer differently:

<h1>Welcome to MY COOL Website</h1>

Then save and commit:

git add .
git commit -m "Updated title locally"

The Collision & Resolution

1. The Crash (Push)

When you try to push, Git panics.

git push
! [rejected] error: failed to push some refs...

2. The Fix (Pull)

Download the conflicting changes.

git pull
CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in index.html

3. The Markers (Open the File)

Open index.html. You will see this mess:

<<<<<<< HEAD
<h1>Welcome to MY COOL Website</h1> =======
<h1>Welcome to the BEST Website</h1> >>>>>>> a1b2c3...

Forking & Pull Requests

How to contribute to open source (e.g., NASA, Facebook) without working there.

  1. Fork: Click the "Fork" button on their GitHub page. This copies their repo to your profile.
  2. Clone & Edit: Download your fork, make changes, and push back to your fork.
  3. Pull Request: Click "New Pull Request". This sends a message to the original owner: "Hey, I fixed a bug. Want to merge it?"

Mastery Notes: Cheat Sheet

The Golden Rule

ALWAYS git pull before you start working!

2. New Commands

git clone <URL> // Download repo
git pull origin main // Update local

3. Resolving Conflicts Workflow

1. git pull // Get conflict
2. Fix code // Delete markers
3. git add .
4. git commit -m "Fixed conflict"
5. git push

learning/github/levels/level4.title: The Time Lord
learning/github/levels/level4.description: Rewriting history, fixing mistakes cleanly, and recovering lost data.
learning/github/levels/level4.html:
Rebase vs. Merge

Merge

Tie two branches together with a knot. It preserves history exactly as it happened (even the messy parts).

Analogy: A truthful diary.

Rebase

Rewrite history to make it look like a straight line. It moves your work to the "tip" of the main branch.

Analogy: A polished resume.

Warning: Never use rebase on a shared branch (like main). Only use it on private feature branches.

The Project (Squashing Commits)

You made 5 messy commits and want to combine them into one perfect commit.

1. Start interactive rebase

git rebase -i HEAD~5

2. The Editor Opens (Change 'pick' to 'squash')

pick a1b2c Added login
squash d4e5f Fix typo
squash g7h8i Forgot semicolon
squash j0k1l Wip
squash m3n4o Final fix

3. Result: Git combines them. You type a new message like "Feature: Login System". History is now clean!

Reset vs. Revert

1. Git Reset (Time Travel)

"It never happened." You jump back in time.

git reset --soft HEAD~1 // Keep files changed
git reset --hard HEAD~1 // Delete changes (Dangerous)

2. Git Revert (The Apology)

"It happened, but I am fixing it." Safe for shared branches.

git revert <commit-hash>

The "Aha!" Moment (Reflog)

You accidentally ran reset --hard and deleted your work. It is not gone. Git keeps a secret diary called Reflog.

// 1. View the secret diary
git reflog

a1b2c HEAD@{0}: reset: moving to HEAD~1
d4e5f HEAD@{1}: commit: My important work

// 2. Rescue the lost commit
git reset --hard d4e5f

Poof! Your deleted files are back.

Cherry-Picking

Sometimes you don't want to merge a whole branch. You just want one specific commit.

git cherry-pick <commit-hash>

Git copies that specific commit and pastes it onto your current branch.

Level 4 Cheat Sheet

1. Clean History (Squash)

git rebase -i HEAD~n

2. Undo Commands

git reset --soft HEAD~1 // Undo commit only
git reset --hard HEAD~1 // DELETE code
git revert <hash> // Safe undo

3. The Savior (Reflog)

git reflog // View history
git reset --hard <hash> // Recover

4. Cherry Pick

git cherry-pick <hash> // Copy commit

learning/golang/days/day01.title: Go Installation & First Program
learning/golang/days/day01.description: Setting up your environment and understanding the anatomy of a Go application.
learning/golang/days/day01.html:
Installation & Verification

Step 1: Install Go

Go to go.dev/dl and download the version for your OS. Follow the standard installation wizard (next → finish).

Step 2: Verify Installation

Open your Terminal or PowerShell and run:

go version

Expected output: go version go1.22.x windows/amd64 (or similar)

Creating the Project

  1. Create a folder: 
    mkdir go-day1
cd go-day1
  2. Create the file:

    Inside the folder, create a file named main.go and paste this code:

    package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
    fmt.Println("Hello, Parsa! Welcome to Go.")
}

Line-by-Line Breakdown

package main

Every Go file starts with a package declaration. main tells Go this is an executable program, not just a library.

import "fmt"

Short for Format. It’s a standard library used for printing text to the console and handling input/output.

func main()

The Entry Point. When you run the program, the computer starts executing instructions from inside these curly braces.

Run & Build

Method A: Quick Run (Development)

Compiles and runs the code instantly without saving a binary.

go run main.go

Method B: Build (Production)

Creates a standalone .exe or binary file you can give to anyone.

go build
# To run the created file:
./main

🧪 Mini Exercise

Modify your main.go file so that it prints the following three lines using multiple fmt.Println calls:

Go is fast.
Go is simple.
Go is powerful.

Hint: You can use fmt.Println() as many times as you want inside the main() function. Each call will start on a new line.

learning/golang/days/day02.title: Variables & Data Types
learning/golang/days/day02.description: Mastering variable declarations, basic types, and the difference between var and := .
learning/golang/days/day02.html:
Declaring Variables

Method 1: The 'var' keyword

Explicit and clear. Used when you want type clarity or are declaring variables outside functions.

var age int = 20
var name string = "Parsa"

Method 2: Short Declaration (:=)

The most common way. Go automatically detects the type.

city := "Toronto" // Go detects string
gpa := 7.75 // Go detects float64

Note: := only works inside functions and cannot be used for reassignment.

Basic Data Types

Type Example Description
int 10 Whole numbers (Integers)
float64 7.75 Decimal numbers
string "Hello" Textual data
bool true Logical true or false

Constants & Clean Code

Constants (const)

Values that never change.

const pi = 3.14
// pi = 3.15 -> Error!

Multiple Declaration

Keep your code idiomatic and clean.

x, y := 10, 20
name, age := "Go", 14

🧪 Mini Exercises

Exercise 1: Profile

Create variables for your name, age, GPA, and a boolean for "likesGo". Print them all using fmt.Println.

Exercise 2: Immutable Graduation

Create a constant graduationYear = 2029. Try to assign it a new value in the next line and observe the compiler error.

Think: Why does age := 20 followed by age := 21 fail? (Answer: := cannot redeclare an existing variable in the same scope.)

learning/golang/days/day03.title: Control Flow in Go
learning/golang/days/day03.description: Mastering program logic using conditional statements, switch cases, and logical operators.
learning/golang/days/day03.html:
The if / else Statement

Basic Conditional

Go conditions do not use parentheses, and curly braces are strictly mandatory.

age := 20
if age >= 18 {
    fmt.Println("You are an adult.")
}

if with Initialization (Go-Style ⭐)

Declare a variable directly in the if statement. It only exists within that scope.

if x := 10; x > 5 {
    fmt.Println("x is greater than 5")
}

Comparison & Logical Operators

Comparison
== Equal
!= Not Equal
> Greater Than
< Less Than
Logical
&& AND
|| OR
! NOT

The switch Statement

Go is cleaner: no break is needed between cases.

day := 3
switch day {
case 1:
    fmt.Println("Monday")
case 2, 3:
    fmt.Println("Tuesday or Wednesday")
default:
    fmt.Println("Invalid")
}

🧪 Mini Exercises

Exercise 1: Number Checker

Write a program that takes a number and prints Positive, Negative, or Zero using if/else.

Exercise 2: Weekday Switch

Create a switch statement that takes a number from 1–7 and prints the corresponding day of the week.

Think: Why is calling fmt.Println(x) outside an if x := 5; ... block invalid? (Answer: x is scoped only inside the if block.)

learning/golang/days/day04.title: Loops in Go
learning/golang/days/day04.description: Understanding all forms of the for loop, flow control with break/continue, and how Go simplifies iteration.
learning/golang/days/day04.html:
The "for" Everything Loop

1. Classic for Loop

The standard initialization, condition, and update pattern.

for i := 0; i < 5; i++ {
    fmt.Println(i)
}

2. for as a "while" Loop

Go does not have a while keyword. Simply omit the initialization and update.

i := 0
for i < 5 {
    fmt.Println(i)
    i++
}

3. Infinite Loop

Runs forever until a break or return is encountered.

for {
    fmt.Println("Running forever")
}

Break & Continue

break

Exits the loop immediately.

if i == 5 {
    break
}

continue

Skips the current iteration.

if i == 3 {
    continue
}

🧪 Mini Exercises

01

Print numbers 1 to 10 using a loop.

02

Print even numbers from 1 to 20. (Hint: use %)

03

Write a loop from 1 to 10 that stops entirely when it reaches 7.

Think: What is the difference between for i:=0; i<5; i++ and for i < 5?

learning/golang/days/day05.title: Functions in Go
learning/golang/days/day05.description: Mastering modularity in Go: parameters, return values, and the superpower of multiple returns.
learning/golang/days/day05.html:
Syntax & Parameters

Basic Function

A simple function without parameters or returns.

func greet() {
    fmt.Println("Hello from Go!")
}

Passing Parameters

Defining specific types for input values.

func greet(name string) {
    fmt.Println("Hello", name)
}

The Go Superpower: Multiple Returns

Go can return more than one value, commonly used for returning both a result and an error status.

func divide(a, b int) (int, bool) {
    if b == 0 {
        return 0, false
    }
    return a / b, true
}

Note: This pattern effectively replaces traditional try/catch exceptions found in other languages.

Named Returns & Scope

Named Return Values

Cleanly define return variable names in the signature.

func rect(w, h int) (area int) {
    area = w * h
    return
}

Function Scope

Variables inside functions are local.

  • Exist only inside the braces
  • Do not affect global state directly

learning/golang/days/day06.html:

%d

var name string
fmt.Print("Enter your name: ")
fmt.Scan(&name)

Interactive Program Example 

switch op {
case "+":

case "/":

package main

    fmt.Print("Enter second number: ")

learning/golang/days/day08.title: Arrays & Slices
learning/golang/days/day08.description: Understanding the core difference between fixed-size arrays and dynamic slices, and mastering the append function.
learning/golang/days/day08.html:
The Big Picture: Arrays vs. Slices

Arrays (Fixed)

Size is part of the type. They cannot grow or shrink once declared.

var nums [3]int
nums = [3]int{10, 20, 30}
Slices (Dynamic)

Flexible size. These are used in 99% of Go code because they can grow.

nums := []int{10, 20, 30}
nums = append(nums, 40)

Slicing Logic

Use the [start:end] syntax to create a sub-slice. Remember: the end index is NOT included.

nums := []int{10, 20, 30, 40, 50}
// Result: [20 30 40]
fmt.Println(nums[1:4])
// Result: [10 20 30] (from start)
fmt.Println(nums[:3])

Length & Capacity

Length (len)

The number of elements currently in the slice.

Capacity (cap)

The total space allocated in the underlying array.

Looping over Slices

The range keyword is the idiomatic way to loop through slices in Go.

for index, value := range nums {
    fmt.Println(index, value)
}

// If you don't need the index, use the blank identifier:
for _, value := range nums { ... }

Create a slice [5, 10, 15, 20]. Append 25 and 30 to it.

02

Critical Concept: Why does append work on slices but fails on arrays? (Answer: Slices are dynamic headers pointing to arrays, while arrays are fixed values.)

learning/golang/days/day09.title: Maps & Range
learning/golang/days/day09.description: Mastering key-value pairs in Go: declaration, manipulation, and the idiomatic way to check for existence.
learning/golang/days/day09.html:
Declaring Maps

Method 1: Using make

The most common way to initialize an empty map.

ages := make(map[string]int)
ages["Parsa"] = 20

Method 2: Map Literal

Declare and initialize with data simultaneously.

grades := map[string]float64{
    "Math": 7.8,
    "CS": 8.4,
}

The "Comma OK" Idiom

In Go, accessing a missing key returns a zero value. Always use the "ok" pattern to check if a key actually exists.

value, ok := grades["Physics"]

if ok {
    fmt.Println("Found:", value)
} else {
    fmt.Println("Key not found")
}

Operations & Iteration

Update & Delete

grades["Math"] = 8.0 // Update
delete(grades, "CS") // Delete

Looping with Range

for key, value := range grades {
    fmt.Println(key, value)
}

Note: Iteration order in maps is randomized and not guaranteed.

Create a map of course → grade. Print all entries using a loop.

02

Use the "ok" pattern to check if "Physics" exists in your map.

03
