Critical Concept: Why is calling grades["Unknown"] directly dangerous? (Answer: Because Go silently returns a zero value, making it hard to tell if the key was actually there.)

learning/golang/days/day10.title: Structs in Go
learning/golang/days/day10.description: Building custom data types to group related data together into clean, real-world objects.
learning/golang/days/day10.html:
Defining & Creating Structs

1. Define the Structure

Group related fields under one name.

type Student struct {
    Name string
    Age int
    GPA float64
}

2. Create a Literal

Initialize values using a struct literal.

s := Student{
    Name: "Parsa",
    Age: 20,
    GPA: 7.75,
}

Slice of Structs

This is the most common pattern in Go for handling lists of objects, like database results or JSON arrays.

students := []Student{
    {Name: "Parsa", Age: 20, GPA: 7.75},
    {Name: "Sara", Age: 21, GPA: 8.2},
}

for _, s := range students {
    fmt.Println(s.Name, s.GPA)
}

Philosophy: Composition over Inheritance

No Classes

Go keeps it simple by avoiding complex hierarchy.

Predictable

Fields are explicit and easy to track.

Composition

Build complex objects by nesting structs.

🧪 Mini Exercises

01

Create a Course struct with Name, Code, and Grade. Instantiate two courses and print them.

02

Create a slice of Student structs, loop over it, and print only the names of students with a GPA over 8.0.

Think: Why does Go prefer structs over classes? (Answer: To promote simplicity and composition over deep, fragile inheritance chains.)

learning/golang/days/day11.title: Pointers in Go
learning/golang/days/day11.description: Understanding memory addresses, referencing vs. dereferencing, and why Go uses pointers for performance and modification.
learning/golang/days/day11.html:
What is a Pointer?

A pointer stores the memory address of a variable instead of the value itself.

Address Operator (&)

x := 10
fmt.Println(&x) // 0xc0000140a8

Dereferencing (*)

p := &x
fmt.Println(*p) // 10

Modifying Original Values

By passing a pointer to a function, you can modify the original variable rather than a copy.

func update(a *int) {
    *a = 100
}

x := 10
update(&x)
fmt.Println(x) // 100

Pointers with Structs

Go automatically handles dereferencing for struct fields, making the syntax very clean.

type Student struct { GPA float64 }

func updateGPA(s *Student) {
    s.GPA = 8.5 // Same as (*s).GPA
}

🧪 Mini Exercises

01

Write a function that takes an int pointer and doubles the value of the original variable.

02

Create a Student struct and a function that updates the GPA using a pointer reference.

Think: Why can you modify slice elements inside a function without using pointers? (Answer: Slices are internally reference types.)

learning/golang/days/day12.title: Error Handling in Go
learning/golang/days/day12.description: Understanding the Go philosophy: errors are values, not exceptions. Master the patterns that keep Go code predictable and explicit.
learning/golang/days/day12.html:
Errors are Values

In Go, error is an interface, not an exception. It is returned like any other value, making flow control explicit.

The Classic Pattern

value, err := someFunction()
if err != nil {
    // handle error
    return
}

⭐ You will see this pattern in almost every Go project.

Creating & Returning Errors

Simple Errors

Use the errors package for static messages.

import "errors"

errors.New("invalid input")

Formatted Errors

Use fmt.Errorf to include variables in your message.

import "fmt"

fmt.Errorf("invalid age: %d", age)

Understanding "nil"

In Go, nil represents "no value". It is the default value for interfaces and errors.

var err error
fmt.Println(err == nil) // true

🧪 Mini Exercises

01

Write a function func sqrt(n float64) (float64, error) that returns an error if the input n is negative.

02

Modify your CLI calculator to return an error for invalid operators or division by zero, and handle it in main.

Think: Why does Go prefer returning value, err over throwing exceptions? (Answer: It makes error handling explicit, predictable, and easier to reason about during code review.)

learning/golang/days/day13.title: Packages & Project Structure
learning/golang/days/day13.description: Understanding how Go organizes code into reusable components and managing dependencies with Go Modules.
learning/golang/days/day13.html:
The Anatomy of a Package

A package is a way to organize code, reuse functionality, and separate concerns. In Go, every .go file belongs to exactly one package, and one folder typically represents one package.

Visibility Rules

  • Exported (Public): Functions or variables starting with a Capital letter are accessible from other packages.
  • Private: Names starting with a lowercase letter are only visible within their own package.

Clean Folder Structure 

go-project/

├── go.mod (Module info)
├── main.go (Entry point)
└── mathutils/
└── mathutils.go (Custom package code)

Go Modules (Required)

To use custom packages and manage dependencies, you must initialize a Go module in your project root.

go mod init go-project

This creates a go.mod file which tracks your module name and versions.

⚠️ Common Beginner Mistakes

  • Circular Imports: Go strictly forbids Package A importing Package B if Package B also imports Package A.
  • Forgetting Init: Trying to import local packages without running go mod init first.

01

02

Initialize a module, import your utils package into main.go, and test the function.

Think: Why does Go force capitalization for exported functions instead of using keywords like public? (Answer: To keep visibility rules simple and explicitly clear directly from the name.)

learning/golang/days/day14.html:

Architecture

student-system/
├── go.mod

    └── student.go

package student

type Student struct {
    ID int

    GPA float64

var students []Student

func UpdateGPA(id int, gpa float64) error {

            students[i].GPA = gpa
            return nil
        }
    }
    return errors.New("student not found")
}
package main

    "fmt"

learning/golang/days/day15.title: Goroutines: Concurrency in Go
learning/golang/days/day15.description: Introduction to Go's lightweight threading model and the fundamental difference between concurrency and parallelism.
learning/golang/days/day15.html:
Concurrency vs Parallelism

Concurrency

Dealing with many tasks at once. It is about structure and managing multiple execution paths.

Parallelism

Doing many tasks at the same time. It is about execution on multiple CPU cores.

“Concurrency is about structure, parallelism is about execution.”

What Is a Goroutine?

A goroutine is a lightweight thread managed by the Go runtime. They are extremely "cheap" to create, allowing you to run thousands simultaneously using the go keyword.

func sayHello() {
    fmt.Println("Hello from goroutine")
}

func main() {
    go sayHello() // Starts concurrently
    fmt.Println("Hello from main")
}

Note: Without synchronization (like time.Sleep or WaitGroups), the program might exit before the goroutine finishes its work.

Advanced Usage

Anonymous Goroutines

go func() {
    fmt.Println("Async task")
}()

Race Conditions

Sharing memory between goroutines without protection is dangerous.

count := 0
go func() { count++ }()

🧪 Mini Exercises

01

Write a program that starts 3 goroutines, each printing a different unique message.

02

Run a loop from 1–10 using goroutines and observe the unpredictable output order in your terminal.

Think: Why is capturing a loop variable i directly inside go func() { fmt.Println(i) }() dangerous? (Answer: All goroutines might reference the final value of the variable instead of the value at the time they were started.)

learning/golang/days/day16.title: Channels in Go
learning/golang/days/day16.description: Mastering communication between goroutines. Learn to synchronize execution and share data safely without shared memory.
learning/golang/days/day16.html:
What is a Channel?

A channel is a pipe that goroutines use to communicate. It allows one goroutine to send values to another, ensuring safe data transfer.

“Do not communicate by sharing memory; share memory by communicating.”

Creating a Channel

ch := make(chan int)
// Channels are type-safe

Send & Receive

ch <- 10 // Send
val := <-ch // Receive

Blocking Behavior

Critical Concept

By default, sends and receives block until the other side is ready. This allows goroutines to synchronize without explicit locks or condition variables.

ch := make(chan int)
ch <- 5 // ❌ Deadlock if no one is receiving!

Synchronization Example

Channels provide a clean way to fix the problem where main() exits before goroutines finish.

func main() {
    done := make(chan bool)

    go func() {
        fmt.Println("Processing...")
        done <- true // Signal completion
    }()

    <-done // Block here until signal received
}

🧪 Mini Exercises

01

Create a goroutine that sends your name to a channel, and have main() receive and print it.

02

Use a loop within a goroutine to send numbers 1–5 to a channel, then receive and print them in main().

Think: Why does ch := make(chan int); ch <- 1; fmt.Println(<-ch) cause a deadlock? (Answer: The send operation blocks the main goroutine before it can ever reach the receive operation. There is no other goroutine to "unblock" the channel.)

learning/golang/days/day17.title: Advanced Channels in Go
learning/golang/days/day17.description: Mastering buffered channels, complex synchronization with select , and advanced concurrency patterns to prevent deadlocks.
learning/golang/days/day17.html:
Buffered Channels

Buffered channels allow sending a limited number of values without a corresponding receiver. This decouples the sender and receiver until the buffer is full.

Capacity & Blocking

ch := make(chan int, 2) // Buffer of 2

ch <- 1 // Doesn't block
ch <- 2 // Doesn't block
ch <- 3 // BLOCKS (Buffer full)

The select Statement

The select statement lets a goroutine wait on multiple communication operations. It blocks until one of its cases can run.

Multiplexing

select {
case msg1 := <-ch1:
    fmt.Println(msg1)
case msg2 := <-ch2:
    fmt.Println(msg2)
}

Timeouts

select {
case msg := <-ch:
    fmt.Println(msg)
case <-time.After(time.Second):
    fmt.Println("Timeout")
}

Fixing the Loop Capture Bug

Passing the loop variable as an argument to the anonymous function ensures each goroutine gets a local copy of the value at that iteration.

for i := 0; i < 5; i++ {
    go func(n int) {
        fmt.Println(n)
    }(i) // Pass i here
}

🧪 Mini Exercises

01

Create a buffered channel of size 3, send 3 numbers into it, and then receive and print them.

02

Use select to listen to two different channels and print whichever one responds first.

Think: Why is select with multiple channels better than multiple if statements for receiving data? (Answer: Because select handles blocking and concurrent readiness of multiple channels safely and efficiently without busy-waiting.)

learning/golang/days/day18.title: sync.WaitGroup & Race Conditions
learning/golang/days/day18.description: Moving beyond time.Sleep to professional synchronization and identifying data safety issues.
learning/golang/days/day18.html:
Professional Synchronization

sync.WaitGroup is the correct way to wait for a collection of goroutines to finish. It tracks a counter that increments when tasks start and decrements when they finish.

func worker(id int, wg *sync.WaitGroup) {
    defer wg.Done() // Decrement counter when done
    fmt.Println("Worker", id, "done")
}

func main() {
    var wg sync.WaitGroup
    for i := 1; i <= 3; i++ {
        wg.Add(1) // Increment before starting goroutine
        go worker(i, &wg)
    }
    wg.Wait() // Block until counter is 0
}

Race Conditions

The Danger of Shared Memory

A race condition occurs when multiple goroutines access the same variable simultaneously and at least one access is a write. This results in unpredictable behavior.

// ❌ DANGEROUS CODE
count := 0
go func() { count++ }()
go func() { count++ }()

go run -race main.go

Use Go's built-in detector!

WaitGroup vs. Channels

Use Case Tool
Waiting for goroutines to finish WaitGroup
Transferring data between goroutines Channels
Orchestrating complex async flows Both (Combined)

🧪 Mini Exercises

01

Start 5 goroutines, each printing its unique ID, and use a WaitGroup to ensure they all finish before the program exits.

02

Refactor your Day 15 concurrency code: remove all time.Sleep calls and replace them with proper WaitGroup synchronization.

Think: Why must wg.Add(1) be called before the go keyword, rather than inside the goroutine itself? (Answer: To prevent a race condition where the main goroutine reaches wg.Wait() before the sub-goroutines even have a chance to increment the counter.)

learning/golang/days/day19.title: Defer, Panic & Recover
learning/golang/days/day19.description: Mastering resource cleanup and Go's unique mechanism for handling unrecoverable errors and program crashes.
learning/golang/days/day19.html:
The defer Keyword

defer schedules a function to run immediately after the surrounding function returns. It is commonly used for resource cleanup like closing files.

LIFO Execution

Deferred functions are pushed onto a stack; the last one deferred runs first.

defer fmt.Println("1")
defer fmt.Println("2")
// Output: 2 then 1

Resource Cleanup

Ensures files or locks are released even if an error occurs.

file, _ := os.Open("t.txt")
defer file.Close()

Panic & Recover

What is panic?

A panic immediately stops execution and crashes the program unless intercepted. Use it only for unrecoverable bugs, never for normal error handling.

panic("unrecoverable state")

What is recover?

recover can stop a panic from crashing the program, but it only works inside a deferred function.

defer func() {
    if r := recover(); r != nil {
        fmt.Println("Recovered from:", r)
    }
}()

panic vs. error

Situation Recommended Tool
Invalid user input error
File not found error
Nil pointer dereference (Bug) panic
Out of bounds array access panic

🧪 Mini Exercises

01

Write a program that uses defer to print "Cleanup Complete" after printing "Processing Data".

02

Create a function that panics if the input number is negative, but use a deferred function with recover to prevent the program from crashing.

Think: Why is using panic for normal control flow (like user validation) discouraged in Go? (Answer: Because it bypasses explicit error handling, makes code harder to follow, and is significantly more expensive in terms of performance.)

learning/golang/days/day20.title: Standard Library Basics
learning/golang/days/day20.description: Exploring Go's "batteries-included" philosophy through core packages for time, OS interaction, and type conversion.
learning/golang/days/day20.html:
The time Package ⏱️

Delays & Measurement

time.Sleep(2 * time.Second)

start := time.Now()
elapsed := time.Since(start)

Key Utility

The time package is essential for handling timeouts in concurrency, measuring performance, and formatting dates.

The os Package (Environment)

Interact with your Operating System by reading environment variables and command-line arguments.

// Read Env Var
db := os.Getenv("DB_NAME")

// Read CLI Args
args := os.Args // [app_name arg1 arg2]

Note: os.Args[0] is always the name of the program itself.

The strconv Package 🔢

Crucial for converting strings to numeric types and vice-versa, especially when handling user input or CLI arguments.

String to Int

strconv.Atoi("42")

Int to String

strconv.Itoa(100)

Parse Float

strconv.ParseFloat("7.5", 64)

🧪 Mini Exercises

01

Write a program that prints the current date and time using time.Now().

02

Create a CLI tool that takes a single number as an argument (os.Args), converts it to an integer, and prints its double.

03

Try to read an environment variable named USERNAME and print a custom greeting if it exists.

Think: Why does Go provide strconv instead of letting you just "cast" a string to an int? (Answer: Because string-to-int conversion can fail, Go forces you to handle the potential error explicitly.)

learning/golang/days/day21.title: Week 3 Review & Parallel Project
learning/golang/days/day21.description: Wrapping up the most powerful features of Go: Concurrency, Channels, and the Standard Library.
learning/golang/days/day21.html:
Week 3 mastery Review

Goroutines & Concurrency
Channels (Buffered/Unbuffered)
sync.WaitGroup & select
Defer, Panic, and Recover

Mini Project: Parallel Data Fetcher

Build a simulation of fetching data from multiple sources (like APIs or Databases) simultaneously using Goroutines and Channels.

func fetchData(id int, ch chan string, wg *sync.WaitGroup) {
    defer wg.Done()
    time.Sleep(time.Second) // Simulate network delay
    ch <- fmt.Sprintf("Data from Source %d", id)
}

func main() {
    results := make(chan string, 3)
    var wg sync.WaitGroup

    for i := 1; i <= 3; i++ {
        wg.Add(1)
        go fetchData(i, results, &wg)
    }

    wg.Wait()
    close(results)

    for res := range results { fmt.Println(res) }
}

Week 3 Graduation

You have mastered the hardest part of Go: Concurrency. You now understand how to build software that is fast, safe, and efficient.

Review: Re-visit the select statement and ensure you understand how it handles timeouts.

Think: Why did we use close(results) in the project code? (Answer: To signal the range loop that no more data will be sent, allowing it to finish gracefully.)

learning/golang/days/day22.title: Go Modules (go mod)
learning/golang/days/day22.description: Mastering dependency management, versioning, and external packages in professional Go environments.
learning/golang/days/day22.html:
What Is a Go Module?

A Go module is the standard way to manage dependencies. It consists of a collection of Go packages stored in a file tree with a go.mod file at its root.

Initialization

go mod init my-project

Managing Dependencies

go.mod

Lists the module path and the specific versions of your dependencies.

module my-project
go 1.22
require github.com/google/uuid v1.6.0

go.sum

Contains cryptographic hashes to ensure dependency integrity across builds.

github.com/google/uuid ... h1:NI...

The go mod Toolkit

Command Purpose
go mod tidy Removes unused deps and adds missing ones.
go mod download Downloads dependencies to local cache.
go list -m all Lists the current module and all dependencies.

🧪 Mini Exercises

01

Initialize a new module named hello-mod in a fresh folder.

02

Import the external package github.com/google/uuid, generate a new UUID, and print it to the console.

Think: Why should you avoid committing a vendor/ folder to your repository unless specifically required by your environment? (Answer: Because go.mod and go.sum already guarantee that everyone on the team will download the exact same versions automatically.)

learning/golang/days/day23.title: HTTP Servers in Go
learning/golang/days/day23.description: Discovering Go's built-in web capabilities. Build production-ready servers using the robust net/http package.
learning/golang/days/day23.html:
The Power of net/http

Go includes a world-class HTTP library in its standard library. Unlike Python or Node.js, you often don't need a framework to build high-performance APIs.

The Basic Loop

func handler(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
    fmt.Fprintln(w, "Hello World")
}

func main() {
    http.HandleFunc("/", handler)
    http.ListenAndServe(":8080", nil)
}

Request vs. Response

Request (*http.Request)

Contains all data sent by the client: URL, Methods, Headers, and Query Parameters.

r.URL.Query().Get("id")

Response (http.ResponseWriter)

An interface used to construct the HTTP response: Status Codes and Body content.

w.WriteHeader(404)

Routes & HTTP Methods

You can define multiple endpoints and restrict them by HTTP Method (GET, POST, etc.).

if r.Method != http.MethodGet {
    http.Error(w, "Only GET allowed", http.StatusMethodNotAllowed)
    return
}

🧪 Mini Exercises

01

Create a simple /ping route that returns the text "pong".

02

Build a /greet endpoint that reads a name query parameter and returns "Hello [name]".

Think: Why does Go's net/http serve production traffic efficiently without a heavy framework? (Answer: Because Go handles each request in its own lightweight Goroutine, allowing it to scale to thousands of concurrent connections with minimal memory.)

learning/golang/days/day24.title: JSON & REST APIs
learning/golang/days/day24.description: Bridging the gap between Go data structures and the web. Master the encoding and decoding of JSON to build modern APIs.
learning/golang/days/day24.html:
JSON Mapping & Struct Tags

Go uses "struct tags" to control how field names appear in JSON output. Fields must be exported (Capitalized) for the JSON package to see them.

type Student struct {
    ID int `json:"id"`
    Name string `json:"name"`
    GPA float64 `json:"gpa"`
}

Encoding & Decoding

Marshal (Struct → JSON)

Converting a Go object into a JSON byte slice.

jsonData, _ := json.Marshal(student)

Unmarshal (JSON → Struct)

Parsing JSON bytes back into a Go struct.

json.Unmarshal(data, &student)

The API Handler Pattern

When building APIs, we use Encoders and Decoders to stream JSON directly from the request and response bodies.

// Sending JSON
w.Header().Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
json.NewEncoder(w).Encode(student)

// Receiving JSON
json.NewDecoder(r.Body).Decode(&s)

🧪 Mini Exercises

01

Create a /students endpoint that returns a hardcoded slice of student structs as a JSON array.

02

Create a POST endpoint that accepts a student JSON object, decodes it into a struct, and prints it to the terminal.

Think: Why does Go require fields to be capitalized (exported) for the json package to work? (Answer: The JSON package uses reflection to inspect the struct; reflection cannot access private/unexported fields.)

learning/golang/days/day27.title: Final Project: Part 1
learning/golang/days/day27.description: Taking everything you've learned to build a professional-grade Student REST API with a multi-layered architecture.
learning/golang/days/day27.html:
Professional Project Structure

Following the "Clean Architecture" principles, we separate our project into layers: the Entry Point, the Domain Models, the Business Logic, and the Web Handlers.

student-api/

├── cmd/server/main.go (App entry point)
└── internal/student/

├── model.go (Data structures)
├── service.go (Business logic)
└── handler.go (HTTP endpoints)

Core Implementation

Service Layer (The "Brain")

This layer handles validation and data persistence, staying independent of the HTTP protocol.

func Validate(s Student) error {
    if s.GPA < 0 || s.GPA > 9 {
        return errors.New("invalid GPA")
    }
    return nil
}

Handler Layer (The "Mouth")

Translates HTTP requests into data the service understands, and formats service results back into JSON.

json.NewDecoder(r.Body).Decode(&s)
w.Header().Set("Content-Type", "application/json")

Testing Your Progress

cURL Test (Create Student)

curl -X POST http://localhost:8080/students -d '{"name": "Parsa", "gpa": 7.75}' -H "Content-Type: application/json"

🧠 Mid-Project Review

Self-Reflection: Why did we use internal/ for the student package instead of putting it in the root? (Answer: To enforce encapsulation. The "internal" directory is a special Go convention that prevents other modules from importing that code, ensuring it stays private to your application.)

learning/golang/days/day28.title: Final CRUD Implementation
learning/golang/days/day28.description: Completing the Student API: Implementing retrieval, updates, and deletions.
learning/golang/days/day28.html:
Service Logic (CRUD) 

func GetByID(id int) (Student, error) {
    for _, s := range students {
        if s.ID == id { return s, nil }
    }
    return Student{}, errors.New("not found")
}

func UpdateGPA(id int, gpa float64) error {
    for i := range students {
        if students[i].ID == id { students[i].GPA = gpa; return nil }
    }
    return errors.New("not found")
}

func Delete(id int) error {
    // Remove element by re-slicing
    students = append(students[:i], students[i+1:]...)
}

Dynamic ID Routing

Handling paths like /students/{id} by trimming the URL prefix.

idStr := strings.TrimPrefix(r.URL.Path, "/students/")
id, _ := strconv.Atoi(idStr)

GET /students/1 (ID)
POST /students (Create)
DELETE /students/1 (Delete)

learning/machine-learning/blocks/block01.title: What Is Machine Learning?
learning/machine-learning/blocks/block01.description: The fundamental shift from writing rules to discovering patterns. Understanding the "Why" before the "How."
learning/machine-learning/blocks/block01.html:
The Core Definition

Machine Learning (ML) is a way of building systems that learn patterns from data instead of being explicitly programmed. In ML, data replaces hard-coded rules.

Traditional

Rules + Data → Output. Humans must define every edge case manually.

ML Way

Data + Answers → Model. The system discovers the rules automatically.

The Learning Loop

"Learning" in ML isn't conscious thought; it's a mathematical optimization process. The goal is to minimize error over time.

1

Prediction: The model makes a guess based on its current internal parameters.

2

Measurement: We compare the guess to the actual answer to see "how wrong" it was.

3

Adjustment: The model tweaks its parameters to perform slightly better next time.

When to use (and NOT use) ML

Use ML When

Rules are complex, you have lots of data, and patterns are hidden.

Avoid ML When

Logic is fixed, data is tiny, or 100% correctness is required (e.g., taxes).

🧠 Mental Model

"Machine Learning is the art of using data to automatically discover patterns that generalize to new situations."

  • ML is applied statistics with massive computation.
  • Success depends on Generalization (performance on new data).

learning/machine-learning/blocks/block01.title: Problem Framing & Data
learning/machine-learning/blocks/block01.description: Most projects fail here, not in the code. Learn to ask the right questions and structure your data for success.
learning/machine-learning/blocks/block01.html:
Features vs Labels

Understanding your inputs (X) and your target (y) is the foundation of any supervised learning project.

Features (X)

The inputs. Information the model looks at to make a decision (e.g., house size, email text).

Labels (y)

The answers. What the model is trying to predict (e.g., house price, spam/not spam).

Mental Rule: Features explain. Labels decide.

The Splitting Strategy

Memorization is not learning. We split data to ensure the model can generalize to data it has never seen before.

Training Set (70%) Used to learn rules
Validation Set (15%) Used to tune complexity
Test Set (15%) Final unbiased evaluation

Data Leakage: The Silent Killer

What is it?

Data leakage happens when information from the future (or the test set) accidentally leaks into training. It leads to fake high accuracy in development, but total failure in the real world.

Example: Predicting a patient's disease using a feature that was recorded *after* the diagnosis was already made.

⚙️ The ML Mindset

  • Objective: What exactly am I trying to predict? (churn? price? cat?)
  • Data: Do I have historical labels (answers) for these features?
  • Evaluation: How will I know if the model is actually learning or just memorizing?

learning/machine-learning/blocks/block01.title: NumPy & Pandas Foundations
learning/machine-learning/blocks/block01.description: Models don't understand reality; they only understand numbers in arrays. Mastery starts with the translators: NumPy and Pandas.
learning/machine-learning/blocks/block01.html:
NumPy: The Math Engine

NumPy is the foundation of every major ML library (Scikit-learn, PyTorch, TensorFlow). It enables Linear Algebra at scale.

Vectorization

Instead of slow Python loops, NumPy applies operations to entire arrays at once. It's faster, cleaner, and mandatory for ML.

Shapes & Dims

A model expects specific structures: (n_samples, n_features). If your shapes don't match, your model can't learn.

Pandas: Thinking in Tables

Pandas is designed for messy, real-world data. It lets you inspect, clean, and filter datasets before they ever touch a model.

Age (X1) Income (X2) City (X3) Churn (y) 2240kToronto0 4590kOttawa1

A DataFrame is just a collection of samples (rows) and features (columns).

The ML Data Flow

1

Load & Inspect

Use Pandas to read CSV/SQL and spot missing values or anomalies.

2

Clean & Reshape

Fix missing data and separate features (X) from labels (y).

3

Convert to Arrays

Models only see NumPy arrays. Convert your DataFrame at the last step.

⚙️ The Translation Rule

Machine learning models learn from numbers, not reality. NumPy and Pandas are your translators. If you get the translation wrong, the model is meaningless.

Beginner Warning: Never feed a string (like "Toronto") directly into a model. Every piece of information must become a float or integer first.

learning/machine-learning/blocks/block02.title: Supervised Learning Deep Dive
learning/machine-learning/blocks/block02.description: Learning by correction. Every classical ML algorithm builds on the relationship between labeled data and optimization.
learning/machine-learning/blocks/block02.html:
The Concept of Supervision

Supervised learning is a mathematical mapping: $X \rightarrow y$. The model learns from labeled data—every input (X) is paired with a trusted "Ground Truth" answer (y).

The Student Analogy

"Think of a student solving math problems with an answer key at the back. Every time they get a problem wrong, they adjust their logic until their answers match the key."

Regression vs Classification

The type of problem is defined by the nature of the output (y). Predicting a price is fundamentally different from predicting a category.

[Image comparing a regression line plot with a classification decision boundary plot]

Regression

Predicts a continuous number on a line.

  • • House Prices
  • • Temperature
  • • Stock Value

Classification

Predicts a discrete category or class.

  • • Spam / Not Spam
  • • Cat / Dog / Bird
  • • Disease / Healthy

The 5 Pillars of Any Supervised System

1

Data (X): Pixel values, word counts, or sensor logs.

2

Labels (y): The ground truth "correct answer."

3

Model: The function that maps $X \rightarrow y$.

4

Loss: The penalty for getting a prediction wrong.

5

Optimization: The method used to change the model and reduce loss.

⚠️ Ground Truth Warning

No algorithm can fix incorrect truth. If your labels are noisy, subjective, or outdated, your model will be fundamentally broken.

"Garbage in, Garbage out."

learning/rust/days/day0.title: Why Rust Exists
learning/rust/days/day0.description: Comparing Python, C++, and Go to understand the unique mission of the Rust programming language.
learning/rust/days/day0.html:
The Core Similarities

Before looking at differences, we must acknowledge that Python, C++, and Go share a fundamental DNA with Rust. They are all General Purpose, support Procedural Logic (Variables, Loops, Functions), and allow for Concurrency.

Logic

All follow the Input → Process → Output model using standard control flow.

Capabilities

All can build CLIs, handle network traffic, and manipulate complex data structures.

Memory Management: The Great Divider

Language Management Style Control
Python Garbage Collection Automatic (Runtime)
Go Garbage Collection Automatic (Runtime)
C++ Manual / RAII Programmer
Rust Ownership System Compile-time

Rust breaks the trade-off: It offers C++ performance without the manual danger, and Python safety without the Garbage Collector pauses.

The Language Philosophies

Python: Speed of writing is king. High abstraction, but slow execution.
C++: Maximum control. Fast, but allows "undefined behavior" and crashes.
Go: Simplicity and concurrency. Easy to learn, but less expressive types.
Rust: Safety first. Forces you to handle every error and memory edge-case before the code even runs.

The Mental Shift

To master Rust, you must unlearn certain habits from other languages:

  • Unlearn "The runtime/GC will clean this up later."
  • Unlearn "I can share this variable across any thread safely."
  • Learn Ownership: Only one part of the code "owns" data at a time.
  • Learn Lifetimes: Explicitly defining how long a reference stays valid.

learning/rust/days/day01.title: Environment Setup & First Program
learning/rust/days/day01.description: Moving from the "Why" to the "How." Today we build your foundation and run your first binary.
learning/rust/days/day01.html:
The Rust Mindset

Rust pushes correctness to compile time. It solves the specific problem of writing fast, low-level code without the typical memory bugs found in C++ or the performance trade-offs of Python.

Python Mindset

"If it runs, we'll see if it breaks."

Rust Mindset

"If it compiles, it is likely correct."

Installing the Toolchain

We use rustup to manage the compiler (rustc) and package manager (cargo).

# Install command for Unix-based systems curl --proto '=https' --tlsv1.2 -sSf https://sh.rustup.rs | sh
rustc --version
cargo --version

Creating Your First Project

Rust expects a structured project layout by default. Use Cargo to scaffold it instantly.

// Create and enter project
cargo new hello_rust
cd hello_rust
// Resulting Structure
hello_rust/
├── Cargo.toml (Metadata/Dependencies)
└── src/
└── main.rs (EntryPoint)

The First Code: src/main.rs 

fn main() { println!("Hello, world!"); }

Key takeaway:

The ! in println! means it is a Macro. Code generation happens here to ensure your formatting is checked at compile-time.

The "Implicit" Test

Unlike Python, Rust allows nothing to exist implicitly. Variables must be declared.

WON'T COMPILE 
x = 5;
RUST WAY 
let x = 5;

learning/rust/days/day02.title: Variables, Mutability & Types
learning/rust/days/day02.description: Understanding how Rust's type system and strict variable rules prevent bugs before they happen.
learning/rust/days/day02.html:
Immutability & mut

In Rust, variables are immutable by default. If you want to change a value, you must be explicit.

// Immutable
let x = 10;

// Mutable
let mut y = 20;
y = 30;

Shadowing vs Mutation

Shadowing allows you to re-declare a variable with the same name, potentially changing its type while keeping the data immutable.

Feature Shadowing Mutation
New Variable? Yes No
Change Type? Yes No
Day 3

Control Flow & Pattern Matching

Mastering match and the power of expressions over statements.

The match Superpower

Rust's match is exhaustive. The compiler ensures you have handled every possible case, preventing "unhandled state" bugs common in other languages.

match number { 1 => println!("One"), 2 => println!("Two"), _ => println!("Anything else"), }

Loops: Safe & Iterative

Rust prefers for loops over iterators to avoid out-of-bounds errors.

Infinite Loop

loop { ... }

Can return values using break.

For Iterator

for item in collection { ... }

No manual index management.

learning/rust/days/day03.title: Control Flow: Logic & Safety
learning/rust/days/day03.description: Mastering match , loops, and why Rust's control flow is fundamentally safer than other languages.
learning/rust/days/day03.html:
if is an Expression

In Rust, if isn't just a statement; it's an expression that returns a value. This allows for cleaner variable assignments based on conditions.

let y = if x > 5 { 1 } else { 0 };
Python: ❌
C++: ❌
Go: ❌
Rust: ✅

Safe Looping Patterns

Rust provides three main ways to loop. The for loop is preferred because it uses iterators, eliminating out-of-bounds risks.

loop

Infinite until break. Can return values.

while

Conditional loop. Standard behavior.

for

Safe iterators. Use 1..4 for ranges.

match: Rust’s Superpower

Matches in Rust are exhaustive. The compiler will not allow you to forget a case, effectively turning logic errors into compile-time errors.

match number { 1 => println!("One"), 2 => println!("Two"), _ => println!("Exhaustive catch-all"), }

Logic Protection

Rust prevents real-world bugs common in other systems languages:

  • C++ Risk Accidental switch fall-through.
  • Rust Fix Match arms never fall through; they are independent.
  • Benefit Enums + Match = Automatic compile-time documentation.

learning/rust/days/day04.title: Functions, Expressions & Return Values
learning/rust/days/day04.description: Mastering the building blocks of Rust logic and avoiding the "Semicolon Trap."
learning/rust/days/day04.html:
Defining Functions

In Rust, function signatures must be explicit. There is no type-guessing for parameters or return values.

fn add(a: i32, b: i32) -> i32 { a + b // Implicit return (no semicolon!) }
  • Parameters must have explicit types.
  • Return type is marked with ->.

Expressions vs Statements

This is the most critical concept for Day 4. Expressions evaluate to a value, while Statements perform an action and return nothing (()).

Expression

5 + 3

Produces 8. No semicolon.

Statement

let x = 5;

Assigns value. Has semicolon.

The Semicolon Trap

Adding a semicolon to the last line of a function changes its return value to Unit (). This is the #1 cause of "Mismatched Types" errors for beginners.

// ERROR: Expected i32
fn x() -> i32 {
  5;
}
// CORRECT
fn x() -> i32 {
  5
}

Scope & Cleanups

Block Scoping

Rust automatically destroys values when they go out of scope. This is why we don't need a garbage collector.

{
  let x = 10; // x is born
} // x is dropped from memory
  • Predictable You know exactly when memory is freed.
  • Efficient No "Garbage Collection pauses" like Python or Go.

thoughts/lessons-from-life.title: Lessons from Life: Growth, Discipline, and The Art of Learning
thoughts/lessons-from-life.html:
"Success is not final, failure is not fatal: it is the courage to continue that counts."

As I navigate my first year of Computer Engineering at York University, I've realized that the most valuable lessons aren't always found in a textbook or a code repository. They are found in the late-night debugging sessions, the challenging exam seasons, and the moments where things just didn't go as planned.

The Power of Discipline

Consistency beats intensity. I used to think that massive bursts of effort were the key to success. However, I've learned that doing the small, boring things every single day is what builds real progress. Whether it's practicing DSA patterns or keeping up with course notes, discipline is the bridge between goals and accomplishment.

Embracing the "Fail Fast" Mentality

In engineering, we often talk about edge cases and failure points. Life is no different. Every mistake is a data point. I've learned to stop viewing failure as a setback and start viewing it as a prerequisite for growth. The faster you fail, the faster you can iterate and improve.

Key Takeaways:

  • Deep Work: High-quality output requires uninterrupted focus.
  • Bias for Action: Don't wait for the "perfect" time. Start building today.
  • Compound Interest: 1% better every day leads to massive results.

Curiosity as a Compass

The world moves fast, especially in tech. Stay curious. Ask "why" more than "how." Understanding the foundational principles makes learning new frameworks and tools significantly easier. Curiosity keeps the journey exciting.

This is an evolving list of reflections. As I continue my journey through university and the professional world, I hope to look back at these notes and see how my perspective has shifted and grown.
